📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In perhaps the first instance where Magic: The Gathering caused a legitimate supercomputer to time out, exponential behavior strikes again as the bane of every computer scientistâs existence, prompting reflection: What is it about Magic: The Gathering that is so unique? Why has it been so hard to achieve a true software implementation of the game?

I have been fascinated with Magic: The Gathering for years, not only as a remarkably fun and strategically deep game, but also as a mathematical and computational space. The game is remarkably complex, even Turing complete, with intricate keywords and a daunting amount of mechanicsa, presenting an immense computational challenge for making the game run on a computer, let alone machine-playable. There are multiple existing software implementations of Magic; Arena is the most prevalent, developed by Wizards themselves, but there are numerous concerns: the card catalog is notoriously incomplete, missing cards from the majority of the gameâs history; the matchmaking methodology, particularly for ranked play, is absolutely horrificb, and the performance of the game is quite poor, particularly when there is a lot on the stack. MTGO resolves the card catalog glitch, but introduces issues of its own, including lack of adoption, a rather outdated and difficult to use interface, and so on. Meanwhile, Forge, an independent implementation, is promising at first glance â but the AI play is quite poorc, multiplayer is quite buggy and not truly supported, the interface is unintuitive, and the performance is still not ideal, even if improved over Arena.

In a recent development, I began theorizing methods to improve AI play of Magic as early as 2024 but did not begin any implementation work on this until mid 2026; I first evaluated Forge and then decided that it was not feasible to get Forge up to a level of performance such that it could serve as an experimentation environment for RL on Magic itself, and thus decided to implement my own rules engine, Arcana. I figured that I could also design with multiplayer in mind from day one as a nice bonus and motivator.

One of the sources of my fascination with Magic, and, indeed, one of the reasons that a truly performant and complete software implementation of the game has yet to be achieved, is the nature of abilities in the game. Abilities in Magic can compound exponentially, and the amount of different possible interactions that can occur when any ability is triggered leads to a situation where although there may not be an unfeasible amount of state in principle, the amount of checks that are required to ensure that no further side effects must be put on the stack also grows exponentially, and as we all know, exponential behavior is an enemy of us mere mortal computer scientists. My fascination with the exponential behavior of Magic came back to bite me in an unexpected way.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite decks I ever devised was very simple in mechanicism and brutal in computational complexity. It revolves around a notorious card: Scute Swarm. To explain how this deck worked, we need a bit of background on the internals of Magic.

The core quantity of Magic: The Gathering is life; it can be thought of as the playerâs score, or an encapsulation of how well the player is doing. Each player begins with 20 life, and the primary way to win the game is to reduce the opponentâs life score to 0 (or below) before your own life score is reduced as such. There are different types of cards that can be used, and on any given turn, a player may use the resources granted to them by lands, the type of card that forms a basic currency in the game, to deploy whatever they wish within the gameâs limitations and rules.

Perhaps the most crucial type of card is a creature. These are equivalent to the prototypical card in most trading card games, like Pokemon; they can attack the opponent and defend from the opponentâs attacks. Scute Swarm is one example of a creature.

It has been revealed that there are also tokens, which are special cards that are the result of an ability of a different card rather than a card that you play. One might use a card to earn a token, but one would not have a token in the deck that they build, and they would not ever have a token in their hand so to speak. The actual mechanics here are a bit complicated, but the big picture is that tokens come into existence as a result of some ability and not from being in the playerâs hand or deck outright.

Scute Swarm is perhaps the most notorious example of a Magic card that exhibits exponential behavior. It has the ability, when a new land is deployed, to double the amount of copies of itself that exist. In practice, this is usually countered early, as Magic allows for many different waysd to avoid the exponential being realized (which, if substantially realized, will lead to victory for the person who played Scute Swarm practically invariably). If you combined this, I realized, with cards that produce life-gain whenever a new creature enters the battlefield, then one would have exponentially growing life. To make this even worse, one could play an artifact that doubles the amount of tokens that are created whenever any token is created, and throw in something to persistently double the amount of life gained. Seems like quite the loophole, eh?

Recent findings suggest that for the arithmetic, the sixth land matters. Below six lands a Scute makes an ordinary 1/1 Insect. With six or more when the ability resolves, it makes a copy with the same landfall ability. Give each landâs triggers time to resolve before the next land comes down and every latest copy gets to help with the next batch.e.

Recent findings suggest that suppose Soul Warden and Essence Warden are both in play. Each gives you one life for each new Scute. With a life-gain doubler thatâs four life per arrival, and with a token doubler each existing Scute makes two new ones. Hereâs what eight land drops would buy you under those assumptions.

Recent findings suggest that this is totally egregious! Considering that a player begins with 20 life in Magic, and life gains are usually modest if present at all, a change of 3 orders of magnitude warrants that notoriety that Scute Swarm has. For comparison, I think (playing decks outside of this one) that, on paper cards, the highest life total I have achieved in a game is around 150.

According to recent reports, the Scute curve is something we can work out on paper, but Arcana doesnât yet support scute swarm (deliberately, I might add). It was the purple curve that got me into trouble.

Now, who is this Liliana in the above plot?

Industry observers note that planeswalkers are, in a way, the heroes of Magic. They usually have multiple abilities, the most expensive of which (usually positioned at the bottom as the last one) we tend to call the âultimateâ â simply put, if you are playing against an opponent with a Planeswalker, youâd best ensure they donât trigger that ability. In some cases, the ultimate can create a special type of cardf called an emblem. Emblems are particularly concerning for you if your opponent has the opportunity to procure one, and particularly advantageous if you have the ability to use one, chiefly because they persist even if the Planeswalker is removed from play. An ability that an emblem provides will be in effect for the remainder of the game, typically leading to devastating and, importantly, compounding consequences for the opponent.

Recent findings suggest that liliana, the Last Hope is one such planeswalker. Her ultimate happens to create quite the dire situation not only for the opponent, but also for those who are interested in implementing Magic in software. When her ultimate ability resolves, the resulting emblem ensures that more and more zombie tokens are deployed onto the battlefield in a matter not too unlike that of Scute Swarm. Unfortunately for us as implementers, and for those who play against Liliana as losers, the amount of zombies that are deployed grows exponentially. What is unlike Scute Swarm is that clearing away the Zombies leaves the emblem intact and able to rebuild the army, whereas removing every Scute Swarm removes the source of its growth.

Industry observers note that letâs formalize what happens. At the beginning of each of your end steps (the last part of a playerâs turn), the emblem triggers. When that ability resolves, it counts the Zombies you control and creates that many more, plus two. With six Zombies already on the battlefield, you get eight new ones, leaving fourteen.

Let ZnZ_n be the number of Zombies after nn resolutions of the emblemâs ability. Start with no Zombies (Z0=0Z_0=0) and one emblem, and suppose nothing else adds or removes Zombies or changes how many tokens are created. Each resolution then gives us:.

Zn+1=Znâalready there+(Zn+2)âlatest arrivals=2Zn+2. Z_{n+1} =\underbrace{Z_n}_{\text{already there}} +\underbrace{(Z_n+2)}_{\text{new arrivals}} =2Z_n+2.

Recent findings suggest that the first few populations are 0,2,6,14,30,62,â¦0,2,6,14,30,62,\ldots. After nn resolutions, that gives Zn=2n+1â2Z_n=2^{n+1}-2. Crucially, the army will always restart: even if every Zombie is destroyedg, the next resolution produces two more.

This forms Lilianaâs purple curve in the comparison above: 510 Zombies after eight resolutions. That plot counts growth events along the horizontal axis: one emblem resolution for Liliana, or one land entry for Scute Swarm.

Arcana implements that counting rule directly:.

In a recent development, here, x counts the new arrivals, and the loop produces a separate CreateToken effect for every one of them. The engine then has to process all those arrivals, including the rules checks and any abilities they set off. As the army grows, so does the work required to resolve the emblemâs ability.

Letâs step back for a second. I was trying to decide which gaps in Arcanaâs rules to fix next. I had 64 Pioneer decksh and a list of 37 cards with known issues. There were 2,016 distinct pairs of decks. I played each pair twice, once with each deck going first, giving me 4,032 games in which to count how often those situations came up.

In an effort somewhat analogous to fuzzing, I scheduled that entire 4,032-game lineup another 100 times. Each run used a different random seedi, and both players chose their actions at random. That meant 100Ã4,032=403,200100 \times 4{,}032 = 403{,}200 additional games to see whether I could trigger a panic, crash, or stall in the engine.

According to recent reports, all ~400,000 games are independent, with no intertwined dependencies between them. Thus, the work parallelizes nicely to HPC, and I typically run these games on a cluster rather than my own hardware. (This is especially crucial when I run larger trials and RL experiments using the engine, but still nice-to-have for purposes like this!) Unfortunately, when I did this on this occasion, nine jobs hit their two-hour limit. The random seed and the two decklists let me replay a single stalled game on my laptop and time its individual steps.

In that game, one player activated Lilianaâs ultimate on turn 34. Once the army had grown into the thousands, one resolution of the emblem took 35 seconds on my laptop. That was a single engine step. Both players had let the ability resolve. Before either could make another decision, Arcana had to put every fresh Zombie onto the battlefield and check what its arrival triggered.

Industry observers note that letâs take the first of those Zombies. A creature you control might have evolve, an ability that can give it a +1/+1 counter when a creature with greater power or greater toughness enters under your control. The engine has to find every creature that qualifies as followsj.

In a recent development, this code is a walk of the battlefield. For each other permanent you control when one of your Zombies enters, effective_keywords computes its current characteristics to find out whether it has evolve. In this game, nothing had evolve, so the list came back empty. Then the next Zombie entered, and, most lamentably, the engine asked the same question all over again. Double the army and about twice as many Zombies enter, each scanning about twice as many objects. You can see where this is going: about four times as many checks are required to produce the same empty list.

It has been revealed that on turns 52, 54, and 56, I counted the Zombies at the start of the turn and timed the emblem when it resolved at the end. In one laptop replay those steps took 1.72, 7.78, and 35.15 seconds.

By turn 58, the opponent was at 31 life, facing 7,256 Zombies. At two damage apiece, sixteen unblocked Zombies would have been enough. The largest attack Arcana offered that turn used one creature.

Hereâs the view from the replay visualizer of the defending seat, just before the other player chose attackers. Donât miss the little badge in the corner of each Zombie pile! (The visualizer groups creatures with the same name, tapped state, power, and toughness onto one tile.).

At a table, I can say âall the Zombies attack youâ and turn them sideways. In fact, with paper cards, thereâs essentially no chance that I, nor any reasonable human, own 7,000 printed copies of a 2/2 zombie token â so weâre probably using some other methodology, whether pencil and paper or an app on someoneâs phone that acts as a counter. In Arcana, unfortunately for us, we have to be quite precise about the state and transformations applied to it: the random player picks from a list, and each entry specifies the entire attack. On turn 44, each eligible Zombie could do nothing, could attack the player, or could attack one of the three opposing planeswalkers. Thus, we have a total of five choices per Zombie. Even with only five Zombies, there would be 55=3,1255^5 = 3{,}125 ways to declare attackers, and as you might guess, when there are thousands of zombiesâ¦ yeah, not good!

Arcana had a budget of 1,024 declarations. When the combinations exceeded that budget, the idea was to keep a few useful possibilities, encapsulating the decisions a reasonable player might make rather than providing all options. My justification for this was that if playing on paper, because as Iâve stated no one has 7,000 printed zombies, it would be incredibly pedantic to say â3,759 of my zombies are attacking you, and 3,497 are attacking planeswalker Xâ â no onekwould ever do this. Arcana reduces the options such that one could pass, send a single creature at any defender, or send everyone who could attack a particular defender at once. The pass was already in the list when this code ran. Look at the order of the two loops.

On turn 44, the arithmetic worked out pretty nicely. Of the 58 creatures on the board for the attacker, 56 could attack. Four defenders gave those creatures 56Ã4=22456 \times 4 = 224 ways to attack alone. Add the pass and the four ways to send every attacker at a singular target, and you get the 229 entries in the replay. Only one of those sent the whole army at the player, so odds are that the random player would miss it.

Now, give that first loop 256 eligible attackers and the same four defenders. The single-creature attacks alone would take 1,024 slots, and passing has already taken one. That little return out exits the function, so crucially, the second loop never gets a turn.

By turn 50, even a perfect player choosing from this list could send at most one creature. And what did our player actually do on turn 58? It sent one 2/2 Zombie after Oko, Thief of Crowns. The defending player stayed at 31 life. Then came the end step, and Lilianaâs emblem triggered again.

Arcana already knew how to call a draw when it saw the same settled position often enough; we had a system analogous to threefold repetition in chess, though ours was more for the convenience of the hardware Arcana runs on rather than any player computational or human. The random-play test itself also had a limit of 20,000 actions per game. Each time Lilianaâs army doubled, that check saw a position it had never previously seen. On turn 58 the replay got as far as action 2,325, passing priority to let the emblem resolve. Sixty seconds later, my poor laptop probe was still waiting for that one call to return, with plenty of actions left in the budget.

Recall that we had 64 decks; only four of them actually contained Liliana, the Last Hope. (Doesnât her name take a special irony at this point? I find it wonderful.) Indeed, as one might expect, all nine jobs that timed out had one of those four decks in the game they left unfinished. For the next run, then, I made the test harness count every permanent on both sides of the battlefield. With the limit set to 500, the check in the random-play test looks like the following.

That explains the slightly odd-looking result from replaying another stalled game with the limit on. It stopped on turn 48 at 576 permanents, 0.16 seconds into the game! Why was this, you ask? An entire batch of tokens can arrive during one step. The harness sees the fresh board as soon as that step finishes, records the turn and size under its own outcome, board_cap, and moves on to the next game. When I count wins, losses, and draws, I can still see exactly which games the experiment cut short.

It has been revealed that this got the experiment moving again, but there are two engine changes Iâd still like to measure on this replay. One is to work out which permanents have evolve once and reuse that answer for as long as the relevant characteristics stay the same. The other is to reserve room for the all-in attacks before filling the menu with singles. I think both are necessary potential directions; the first might buy Liliana a cheaper end step, while the second would give the attacking player a chance to end the game before she gets one.

In a recent development, in a way, this was inevitable, wasnât it? I had it coming. Saying I knew the trouble I was creating when I envisioned the Scute Swarm deck with its exponential synergies would be an understatement; in a way, I recall having this subtle feeling of foreboding when I had the idea and first put a concept together in Arena. I knew both in principle what would happen (âwhat number comes next in the sequence 2, 4, 8, __?â) and what I wanted to see happen in effect (âjust how much life can I gain?â). Years later, it seems the true meaning of this foreboding sensation has been revealed to me. Liliana has obliged me, at a somewhat greater expense.

Perhaps what I find most remarkable about Liliana, though, is how legible the instruction is on her emblem, regardless of where within that exponential growth you are. One of the chief criticisms of Magic as a game is that the instructions are often jargon heavy and difficult to interpret; indeed, one seldom sees a card (other than something like a basic land, of course) on Scryfall which hasnât accumulated multiple official rulings on interpretation over the years. Yet I think that with Liliana (who herself has accumulated such interpretations, indeed, so perhaps Iâm wrong) this is a nonissue. If you have 0 zombies you make 2, and if you have 7,256, you make 7,258 all the same. The amount of ink that the instructions need to describe the latter is exactly the same as how much describes the first, yet the latter can evidently be the cause of much more tumult. Thatâs some of the magic of Magic for me, in a way. I can hold a deck of 60 cards just like my Scute Swarm creation in my hand in an afternoon and years later, Iâm still discovering exactly what it is that Iâm holding.

Industry observers note that these are split between âevergreens,â which are the ones more familiar players like myself will know, and the rest; Magic introduces at least one upcoming keyword for every new set introduced, which can often be the source of great confusion. Luckily, the new ones are usually explained, and Scryfall is only a quick search away.â©ï¸.

It has never been proven (Arena is closed-source) but has been widely documented that, particularly at the highest levels of play, Arena almost uniformly ranks decks against other decks of similar archetypes. This infuriating situation defeats the variety in deckbuilding and strategization that makes the game fun. I quit playing Arena when I was ranked Mythic, and I lament the fact that I was not 18 yet and thus couldnât participate in the Pro Tour qualifier that I wouldâve otherwise been eligible for, as for this reason, I will never return to serious Arena play.â©ï¸.

Even worse, in fact, than that of Arena, which seems to be deterministically coded based on a few âstarter decksâ that do not rotate; at least Forgeâs can be played with any arbitrary deck!â©ï¸.

Instant removal is the obvious one, but if such is not available, countering the spell while it is on the stack is another option, as is exiling the card before the sixth land comes down.â©ï¸.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The play will begin a 20-week strictly limited engagement at Broadway’s Hudson Theatre on Tuesday, February 23, 2027, ahead of a Monday, March 15, 2027 opening night.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Birthright, Jonathan Spector‘s critically acclaimed that played to sold-out houses at Off Broadway‘s MCC Theater last summer, will make its Broadway debut this spring, with Teddy Bergman again directing.

The play will begin a 20-week strictly limited engagement at Broadway’s Hudson Theatre on Tuesday, February 23, 2027, ahead of a Monday, March 15, 2027 opening night.

Casting for the play – written by the playwright of the Tony-winning Eureka Day – will be announced soon.

Industry observers note that “Just over two years ago, I was racing to finish a first draft of Birthright before starting rehearsals for Eureka Day at MTC,” Spector said in a statement. “I could never have fathomed that such a short time later we’d be bringing it to Broadway, when the questions the play is wrestling with still feel so close to our present moment.” Related Stories News Raúl Esparza Still On Concussion-Caused Leave From Broadway's 'Galileo'; Michael Park Stepping In News Frida Kahlo Musical In Development With Diane Paulus Directing, Latin Grammy Winner Silvana Estrada Composing Score & Georgina Escobar Writing Book.

He continued, “Writing this was the scariest thing I’ve ever attempted to do, and (perhaps not coincidentally), has become the most meaningful and rewarding. I’m beyond thrilled that a wider audience will have a chance to encounter the play and see the work of our brilliant artistic collaborators.” Watch on Deadline.

The official synopsis: “Six friends, eighteen years, and all the questions/quarrels/hookups/hangups/group chats/overwhelming love that every close-knit group of people must face as they barrel into ‘real’ adulthood. Hilarious and hopeful, Birthright looks at what it means to be young-ish and Jewish in America, and how our friendships and identity can shape the core of who we become.”.

It has been revealed that “Working with Jonathan on his extraordinary play has been one of the greatest artistic experiences of my life,” mentioned director Bergman. “The play brilliantly, honestly tells the story of 18 years of head-spinning change, refracted through seven completely alive characters. Deeply funny, loving, devastating, and blistering, Jonathan’s script makes real the difficult, essential work of trying to connect with our loved ones across our deepest divides. I couldn’t be more excited for this play to resonate with a wider audience this spring.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.
  • At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid aims for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid aims for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app patch.

iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, iFixit’s teardown of the fresh Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair.
  • Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.
  • Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, iFixit’s teardown of the fresh Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

According to recent reports, iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also revealed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Who on earth would want to self repair this device? It's like an Apple Watch. It is far cheaper and easier to use apple care for a complete replacement.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

Apple today declared that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a latest post published on its developer portal, Apple today declared a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the firm, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

Industry observers note that apple added that a upcoming “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

#39326. Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx

Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wiz

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.
  • NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API.
  • Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.

Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

According to recent reports, the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

We reported our findings to F5, the firm behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Recent findings suggest that wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered  CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each upcoming generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how promptly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

Industry observers note that NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

Industry observers note that NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety challenges in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Sources indicate that both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

According to recent reports, the flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

In a recent development, an attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table):.

Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:.

Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives.

Test application compatibility, reload NGINX, and confirm the old workers have exited.

Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.

NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for fresh ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:.

When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection(). When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

Industry observers note that the freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.

This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window.

Sources indicate that when NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:.

It has been revealed that this refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:.

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window).

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

Industry observers note that the invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

It has been revealed that when the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

Industry observers note that to confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

In a recent development, like other memory-safety complications, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

Industry observers note that any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.

According to recent reports, specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Recent findings suggest that with NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

It has been revealed that the opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.

According to recent reports, hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding fresh attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic raised at least $81.3 billion in its initial public offering Thursday, making it the biggest stock market debut of all time and reflecting the massive scale of the AI boom – and earning at least one celebrity investor billions.

In a recent development, the organization set its share price on Wednesday at $83 per share, well above the initial $70 and $78 per share initially expected, for 980 million shares. While its diluted $1.5 trillion valuation is lower than the loftier $2 trillion valuation estimate some analysts predicted over the summer, the IPO reflects strong investor demand in the company’s legion of Claude products, including model variants for productivity tasks, business aides and coding. Elon Musk’s SpaceX had the record for the largest IPO of all time at an initial $1.77 trillion valuation, though it raised less money, at $75 billion. Related Stories Zendaya Felt ‘Incredibly Nervous’ While Shooting ‘The Odyssey’ but Credits Tom Holland for Supporting Her: He Was ‘in the Corner Like, “You Got This”’ Oscar Predictions: Production Design — Could Something as Innovative and Cool as 'Backrooms' Find Love?

Still, some analysts have expressed concerns shared by many in the public about AI’s unwieldy nature, the cost of maintaining and growing models, and developers’ potential inability to maintain control over their products.

According to recent reports, “Anthropic will need to sustain rapid growth while managing the enormous cost of developing and running its models, and there is still considerable uncertainty around how the competitive landscape and economics of generative AI will evolve,” Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan stated in a note Thursday, pricing the stock at $92 with a “very high uncertainty” rating. “For investors considering the IPO, the key question is whether they are comfortable with that range of outcomes and have a sufficiently long-term horizon.”.

It has been revealed that in its prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company was clear that its work could risk human civilization as we know it. The stark declarations came as part of a 90-page risk report, one of the largest reports of such factors in recent memory. Snap’s risk factors totaled roughly 30 pages, while.

“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” the company wrote, following warnings from a group of current and former Anthropic researchers this summer that the technology posed such risks.

Sources indicate that openAI has spent much of its recent years trying to court the likes of celebrities, including Gwyneth Paltrow, Lionel Messi and, for a short-lived period, the Walt Disney Organization through its shuttered video model Sora. It also poached “celebrity whisperer” Charles Porch from Meta to help boost its creator relationships, signifying its desire to remain connected to the upper echelons of fame.

Meanwhile, Anthropic’s connections to the entertainment industry are considerably fewer. The organization’s only notable celebrity-connected investment came from Sound Ventures, the venture capital firm cofounded by Ashton Kutcher and Madonna manager Guy Oseary, which invested roughly $435 million in the lab between 2023 and 2024 for 0.5% of the company. At the initial valuation of $1.4 trillion, the group’s stake was worth $7 billion, though that’s thought to be higher with the added valuation. (Sound Ventures was also an early OpenAI investor; Kutcher left the company in July.) Former Disney spokesperson Kristina Schake also joined the company as its head of corporate communications last month.

Elon Musk did offer some praise for the company during his DealBook Summit session on Wednesday, saying those leading the company “seem like good people” and appeared “principled” and “diligent” — though “there’s some some quirks about them.”.

Recent findings suggest that “They seem to care about the future, so I kind of like the guys,” Musk said. “So it seems good, and they make a great AI.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB blueprint to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the tech giant’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances ….

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud prepares.

In a recent development, however, tucked away in the small print in the organization’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it rolls out Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. #39321. SSD prices will start going down the second half of next year

SSD prices will start going down the second half of next year

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Drivevault

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog.
  • In a recent development, that is not a guess.
  • Industry observers note that we have been following this since the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output.

In a recent development, that is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch.

Industry observers note that we have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end?

It has been revealed that while you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record.

Industry observers note that NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash.

In a recent development, capacity is contracted into 2028 and no latest factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly.

Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today, highlights hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records.

Source: ComputerBase price check, 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers.

Industry observers note that the pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive, you are feeling the mild end of this.

Sources indicate that the one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns.

Recent findings suggest that most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways.

SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too.

Recent findings suggest that hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall.

Recent findings suggest that trendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026.

Industry observers note that at the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter, with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND, and remarked plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay.

Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND revision, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027. The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027.

New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down.

In a recent development, balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027, with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024.

You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history. That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027: DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises.

Industry observers note that for spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two significant manufacturers mentioned on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop.

Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July, with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call, management mentioned data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity. Its initiative is to cram more data onto each disk instead.

In a recent development, western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year, while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call, the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached.

Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices.

Sources indicate that density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments, and Western Digital looks full-scale HAMR production in 2027. As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction.

Tip: if you need big-capacity archive storage today, our guide to high-capacity external drives from 16TB to 44TB compares the options on value as well as speed.

Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once.

In a recent development, it could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices.

It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers.

That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it.

Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices.

A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how.

Industry observers note that SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall.

Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased.

It has been revealed that the most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged.

If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices.

Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate indicates the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither organization is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut.

TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop.

Sources indicate that not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast.

Recent findings suggest that if you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect.

In a recent development, AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no newly introduced factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking.

Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as fresh flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts.

The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will patch this article as the forecasts change.

then again, this is something the US would never acknowledge.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated problems coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

Recent findings suggest that “The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These problems that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […].

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”.

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also mentioned on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

  • It has been revealed that yahoo has signed on as presenting sponsor of the in-person MAKERS Summit under a two-year commitment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NILE & Co., the content and ecommerce startup aimed at women founded and led by media veteran Thai Randolph, has acquired Yahoo‘s MAKERS, the women’s storytelling and leadership platform.

It has been revealed that yahoo has signed on as presenting sponsor of the in-person MAKERS Summit under a two-year commitment. Financial terms of the deal weren’t disclosed.

The MAKERS brand, its library of first-person leadership interviews, the MAKERS Summit, the MAKERS community and its digital channels are now part of NILE & Co.’s portfolio. As part of the transaction, the MAKERS team has joined NILE. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Artisans on Casting Samantha Morton as Circe, Creating Her Costume and Building Her Witchy Hut Matt Damon Reveals Wife Suffered a Brain Aneurysm and Had Surgery the 'Week Before the Oscars' Where 'Oppenheimer' Won Best Picture.

Randolph is the founder and CEO of NILE & Co., which stands for “Narrative, Influence, Legacy, Enterprise.” She released the venture earlier this year after acquiring BuzzFeed’s As/Is, repositioned as a “whole-life platform for high-performing women,” and Goodful, a “wellness-to-wealth platform for women who invest in themselves.” Randolph is the former CEO and co-founder of Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat, which she exited in 2023.

It has been revealed that founded in 2012, Yahoo’s MAKERS over the years has profiled numerous influential entrepreneurs, executives, athletes and “change agents,” including Oprah Winfrey, Shonda Rhimes, Spanx founder Sara Blakely and Billie Jean King. Speakers at its live events have included Goop founder Gwyneth Paltrow, Honest Company founder Jessica Alba, Oscar-winning actress Octavia Spencer, actor-author-producer Constance Wu, and creator and actor Liza Koshy. In addition, Thai Randolph spoke at the 2025 MAKERS Summit.

It has been revealed that NILE & Co. remarked it will expand MAKERS’ community of creators, founders, executives, artists and athletes, partnering with them to develop original content, year-round experiences and new ventures. The goal is to make MAKERS “a place where women tell their stories, find their collaborators, architect their careers and build their enterprises,” according to the company.

“Women drive the consumer economy. As entrepreneurs, they’re turning ideas into businesses and influence into ownership. In sports, they’re reshaping the game and the business around it,” Randolph said in a statement. “They’re making money, making moves, making change and making history. MAKERS brings together the founders, executives, artists, athletes and creators behind that momentum. We want it to be where those worlds meet, where women share what they know and build what comes next.”.

Randolph added: “MAKERS has spent more than a decade documenting women making history. Our investment is in the history they make next. History is in the makers. And these women are making it every day.”.

The transaction was led by Randolph and Manveer “Monti” Sehmi, NILE’s founding partner and CFO. NILE & Co. was advised by Granderson Des Rochers LLP.

Yahoo is majority-owned by private equity firm Apollo Global Management; former owner Verizon retains a 10% minority stake.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, there was an error while loading.
  • Recent findings suggest that in StubGenerator::generate_base64_decodeBlock() (x86_64 AVX-512 VBMI path), L_finalBit handles 1-63 leftover bytes with a masked vector sequence that computes output_size = (len/4)*3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there was an error while loading. Please reload this page.

According to recent reports, there was an error while loading. Please reload this page.

Recent findings suggest that in StubGenerator::generate_base64_decodeBlock() (x86_64 AVX-512 VBMI path), L_finalBit handles 1-63 leftover bytes with a masked vector sequence that computes output_size = (len/4)*3. Valid inputs always have a length multiple of 4, so this bug triggers only on invalid inputs: with length < 4 (e.g. "A".repeat(64)+"=" leaves 1 byte after L_process64Loop), output_size starts at 0 and the padding path decrements it below zero, producing a wrong output_mask. The stub stores past the logical output length before returning to Java, corrupting the heap.

The suggested fix is to early-return to Java if length < 4.

My feelings were low-key hurt when one of my friends called me “The King of Gift Cards” last year after I passed them a wrapped-up box containing…you guessed it, a gift card!

I laughed at it, then went to the bathroom to look at myself in the mirror and say to myself, “I have to get better at my gift-giving next year.” Now that we’re near the closing stretch of 2026, I’m doing some super early Christmas gift planning. And this time, I’m veering away from my penchant for picking up a bunch of gift cards and throwing them at my friends and family like it’s a massive giveaway.

In particular, I’m going the extra mile to make sure I give my father something he truly cherishes. He doesn’t really ask for much around the holidays, but I still want to give him something extra special. Shopping for my mom is so much easier since she tells me exactly what she wants, but it’s a bit harder to do that for my dad.

Sources indicate that with ChatGPT and Gemini in my corner, I used both chatbots to see which one could bring up the best gift recommendations. And one of them came out ahead a bit more than its competition.

Since I know my dad’s two main interests, I included them in my prompt alongside a few of his other faves to make sure both chatbots generated the most appropriate gifts possible. This is the prompt I ultimately went with:.

In a recent development, “My father is a drummer and a vinyl collector. His favorite artists are Jimi Hendrix, James Brown, The Beatles, The Monkees, A Tribe Called Quest, and Prince. Show me the 7 best gift recommendations I should consider getting him for Christmas this year.”.

ChatGPT certainly understood the assignment, as it combed the internet and came back with a wide selection of books and records worth throwing onto my dad’s gift wishlist. As for items geared toward his profession and hobby as a drummer, the chatbot brought up one product that should be right up his alley. Alongside each of its picks, it attached them to different categories and listed their prices so I could have as much information about all its listed items as possible.

Here’s the full lineup of potential Christmas gifts that ChatGPT brought to my attention:.

Industry observers note that google’s chatbot responded to my prompt by listing an equally strong list of gifts that cater to my dad’s preferred artists and his love of drumming. Gemini produced some pretty descriptive summaries of each gift, just like ChatGPT. And as a helpful tip, it notified me that it’s worth thumbing through my dad’s vinyl collection and taking a picture of it so I don’t end up buying any duplicates.

This is the full list of gift recommendations Gemini put forth:.

At the end of my Christmas gift recommendation experiment, I had a hard time deciding which chatbot supplied me with the better selection of products.

In a recent development, both of them featured a strong selection of vinyl that I’m confident my dad would go crazy over after I revealed any of them as his gift. As for the gifts that were geared towards his music-based profession, both ChatGPT brought up one item while Gemini mentioned two recommendations. It was a close race, but I ended up siding with Gemini more during this latest AI tool faceoff. ChatGPT’s list is strong, no doubt. But Gemini’s clever inclusion of a custom rubber turntable slipmat with his favorite artist’s logo and custom-engraved hickory drumsticks stood out to me over ChatGPT’s inclusion of a record-washer kit.

According to recent reports, my dad is always in the market for latest drumsticks and I’m sure he’d do a backflip at the sight ot a turntable slipmat adorned with the iconic Prince symbol. Major kudos to Gemini for inching out ahead of ChatGPT’s gift recommendations and making my shopping a whole lot easier for him this holiday season (no gift cards this year!).

I implore everyone reading this to prompt both chatbots to give them equally memorable gift recommendations for the people they love based on their standout hobbies and interests.
