💡 Key Takeaways
  • After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today.
  • When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the organization described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.
  • In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the organization described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Consumers can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Industry observers note that beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets people block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets owners quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

In a recent development, as MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, owners can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

“When we introduced Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

Check out Moonlock for iPhone on the App Store.

John Legend has sung “The Star-Spangled Banner” at the World Series, the NBA Finals and the NBA All-Star Game. After going pro, he’s turning to college sports.

ESPN has tapped the popular musician to draw attention to the looming College Football Playoff, which kicks off on Friday, December 18. In a fresh promo that beings airing Thursday, Legend offers a musical number with what he calls “Rat Pack energy” to highlight the fact that t post season play will end in Las Vegas with the CFP National Championship. Related Stories Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of 'Kaante' and 'Zinda,' Dies at 59 Oscar Predictions: Production Design — Could Something as Innovative and Cool as 'Backrooms' Find Love?

“it was easy for me to pick that as the musical direction, he tells Variety, because he’s a fan of Frank Sinatra, and extremely familiar with his music, “That was my North Star for where I was going.”.

This sort of performance “is just a different challenge” Legend says. “You can’t do lots of repetition, but you have to make it hooky, and that was the compositional challenge. “He found the process fun, “because I think sometimes constraints make creativity easier in some ways. You have the boundaries. It’s like coloring within the lines rather than just drawing something freehand.

ESPN has fresh reason to call attention to post-season college football. It will soon be showing a lot more of it. The Disney sports-media giant will be the exclusive worldwide rightsholder to an expanded 24-team College Football Playoff, starting with the 2027-28 season. ESPN gets media rights to eight CFP first round games, eight CFP second round games, four CFP quarterfinals, two CFP semifinals and the CFP national championship — compared with 11 games in the current 12-team Playoff.

“John Legend is the perfect fit for this campaign,” said Maggie Lewin, ESPN senior director of marketing. “He is a true college football fan. He can truly talk the talk, while also bringing a sense of showmanship and entertainment value to the spectacle of the CFP in Vegas this year. The campaign is bold, fun and a little wild – making it the perfect message for this year’s CFP.”.

Legend’s only complaint? There’s a “sad irony” to the project. His favorite team is fighting to keep its post-season dreams alive. Legend is a fan of Ohio State, which just broke a two-game losing streak.

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL rolled out on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial upgrade.

According to recent reports, on Android, this comes in the form of newly introduced color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Sources indicate that colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

It records in 2K resolution and runs on a rechargeable battery, while support for microSD storage lets you save footage locally without paying for a cloud subscription.

Sources indicate that reolink’s 4K Solar Security Camera is down to $144.99 from $229.99, saving you $85. It connects over 4G LTE, so it can keep watch over a barn, vacation home, construction sites, or other areas where a regular wifi security camera won't work because there’s no home network to join. Sources indicate that eufy’s SoloCam S340 is $119.99, down from $219.99, and it pairs a 3K wide-angle lens with a 2K telephoto lens, giving you a view of the whole yard and a closer look at faces or packages at the same time. The camera pans a full 360 degrees and tilts to follow people as they move, and the included solar panel keeps it charged in a sunny spot. Footage is stored on 8GB of built-in storage with no monthly fee—one of the reasons why the S340 earned an Editors’ Choice award in PCMag’s review.

Eufy’s Video Doorbell E340 is $99.99, down from $169.99, and it uses two cameras to cover your front door, with one recording visitors in 2K and the other pointing down at the doorstep to keep an eye on deliveries. It also has color night vision, a removable rechargeable battery, and 8GB of built-in storage for recording footage without a cloud subscription. You can read more about its performance in PCMag's review.

At $28, down from $79.99, the second-generation Arlo Wireless Video Doorbell 2K is one of the more affordable ways to keep an eye on your front door. Its 2K camera provides a detailed view of visitors, while the wide field of view helps capture packages left near your doorstep—making it easy to see why PCMag named it the best video doorbell of 2024.

It has been revealed that the Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ is down to $34.99 from $79.99. It records in 2K resolution and offers a head-to-toe view, so you can see who's at the door as well as any packages left on your doorstep. And since it runs on batteries, installation is relatively simple, especially for renters or anyone who doesn't want to deal with doorbell wiring. For more on it, check out PCMag’s review.

Recent findings suggest that the Eufy Security FamiLock E34 is down to $179.99 from $279.99, saving you $100 on a smart lock that uses palm vein recognition to unlock your door, which Eufy says takes just 0.6 seconds. It can store palm data for up to 50 people locally, making it convenient for households with multiple owners, while PIN codes and app-based controls give you other ways to get inside. You also get built-in wifi and compatibility with Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home, and Matter.

Sources indicate that the Ultraloq Bolt Fingerprint smart lock is $139.99, down from $199.99, and it replaces your deadbolt with a lock you can open using a fingerprint, a keypad code, or the U Home app over built-in wifi. It can also unlock automatically as you walk up to the door, using your phone’s location. PCMag named it the best smart lock of 2024.

Industry observers note that simpliSafe’s DIY 8-piece Wireless Home Security System is down to $119.99 from $209.99, making it a relatively affordable starting point for securing multiple entry points around your home. The kit includes a base station, keypad, entry sensors, a motion sensor, and a panic button, so you can monitor doors, windows, and movement inside the house. For more details, check out PCMag’s in-depth review.

The Arlo Home Security System is $142.49, down from $199.99, and this starter kit pairs a Keypad Sensor Hub with two All-in-One Sensors, each of which can be set to detect motion, open doors and windows, water leaks, and other events across eight functions. It runs in the same Arlo Secure app as Arlo’s cameras and doorbells, which makes it a natural addition for homes that already use them. For more on its features and performance, check out PCMag’s review.

Industry observers note that at just $15.99, down from $39.99, the Blink Mini 2K+ is one of the cheapest ways to add indoor monitoring to your smart home. This compact plug-in camera records in 2K resolution, and also supports motion alerts, two-way audio, and Alexa integration. PCMag has a review of the Blink Mini 2K+.

Industry observers note that the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is seeing a substantial discount, dropping from $59.99 to $24.99. It records in 2K resolution, giving you a clear view of rooms and hallways, while two-way audio lets you speak to family members or pets through the Ring app. There's also a built-in privacy cover that blocks the camera when you don't want it recording, along with support for other Ring and Alexa devices. You can read more about its features and performance in PCMag's review.

According to recent reports, arlo’s Essential Pan Tilt Indoor Cam 2K is $18.99, down from $49.99, and it’s part of the lineup Arlo released in 2025, with a motorized head that rotates a full 360 degrees and tilts 180 degrees so one camera can cover an entire room. This PCMag review goes into more detail on how it performs.

The Sensi Smart Thermostat ST55 is right now $79, down from $129.99, and is a good option for anyone looking to control their home's heating and cooling from a phone—it lets you create schedules, adjust temperatures remotely, and use geofencing to make changes based on whether you're home or away. It also works with several popular smart home platforms, including Alexa, Google Assistant, and Samsung SmartThings, plus Apple HomeKit when a C-wire is connected, notes this PCMag review.

Sources indicate that the Amazon Smart Thermostat is a more affordable alternative at $56.99, down from $79.99. It works with Alexa to let you adjust temperatures through voice commands or the Alexa app, where you can also set schedules and automate temperature changes based on your routines. For more on its setup and features, check out PCMag's review.

Ecovacs’ Deebot X8 Pro Omni is down to $699.99 from $1,099.99, saving you $400 on a robot vacuum that takes care of both vacuuming and mopping. It uses a roller mop that continuously rinses itself with clean water as it works and extends outward to clean along walls and furniture. You also get 18,000Pa of suction and a self-maintaining dock that empties the dustbin, washes the mop with hot water, and dries it afterward. For more on its cleaning performance, check out PCMag’s review.

It has been revealed that the Roborock Qrevo CurvX has dropped to $799.99 from $1,499.99, saving you $700. It’s a 2025 update to the Qrevo Curv that raises suction from 18,500Pa to 22,000Pa and slims the robot to 3.14 inches tall so it fits under more couches and beds, while keeping the AdaptiLift chassis for climbing thresholds and a dock that washes the mop pads with hot water. This PCMag review covers the original Qrevo Curv, which should be a useful reference for the design and dock the two models share.

Anthropic logo, Guilherand-Granges, France, March 2025.

It has been revealed that anthropic’s shares start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday as ANT. Grey markets point to a strong start. Derivatives offered by the broker IG implied a gain of about 27% on the $83 Anthropic IPO price, Bloomberg reported.

Industry observers note that perpetual futures tied to Anthropic on the Hyperliquid blockchain changed hands at around $105, a similar premium. Nasdaq 100 futures were up 2.1% at 6am in New York.

“I’d expect healthy demand at the open, and volatile but strong performance through the day,” Hans Stege, head of investment research at PrePublic Equity Partners, told Bloomberg. “But that’s maybe the easy part, ask me again in three weeks.”.

US listings this year have fallen a weighted average of about 4%, according to Bloomberg’s data.

Sources indicate that anthropic confirmed the $83 price in its own announcement on Wednesday night. The organization is selling 956.4m shares, and existing stockholders another 23.6m. Together with the private placement, the deal raised a record $107.3bn.

The underwriters have 30 days to buy up to 147m more shares, worth about $12.2bn at the IPO price. The offering is due to close on Friday.

At $83 a share, Anthropic’s 5,300 employees will hold about $232bn in stock. CNBC’s Robert Frank worked that out from the filings. That works out at an average of $44m each.

Sources indicate that more than 400 early employees will be worth $100m or more, investors told CNBC. Each of the seven co-founders holds between 230m and 240m shares, about $20bn apiece. Lockups and vesting schedules mean much of that wealth stays on paper for now.

It has been revealed that staff hired before 17 May 2024 can pledge up to half of their vested shares to charity. Anthropic matches each dollar three times. The co-founders have already pledged 80% of their equity.

Anthropic sold $1.1bn of stock to retail investors in the UK and continental Europe, Bloomberg reported from regulatory filings. UK savers took just over 3.6m shares, and buyers in the EU, Norway, and Switzerland close to 9.7m. SpaceX sold $364m to UK savers in June.

In a recent development, facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz helped fund Anthropic’s first round in 2021. He has now distanced himself from the firm.

Recent findings suggest that “Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,” he said in a statement to The Upcoming York Times. “A.I. is moving too fast. Anthropic and everyone else on the frontier should slow down and stop racing.”.

Sources indicate that he and his wife, Cari Tuna, moved their stake into a nonprofit in early 2025. That way they would not profit from selling it, a spokesman told the paper. On Wednesday, a coalition of scientists and tech figures signed a statement calling Anthropic not a safe AI manufacturer, the MisAnthropic Statement.

Breaking: Santa appeared 70,778 times in 2026’s breached passwords, Specops finds

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that “Santa” turned up 70,778 times in passwords exposed this year, according to newly introduced research from Specops, the Swedish password security company owned by Outpost24.
  • According to recent reports, the analysis, published today on the Specops blog, covered more than 260 million breached passwords from 2026.
  • The research team searched for 26 holiday and seasonal terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Santa” turned up 70,778 times in passwords exposed this year, according to newly introduced research from Specops, the Swedish password security company owned by Outpost24. That is more than 25 times as often as “christmas”, which appeared 2,796 times.

According to recent reports, the analysis, published today on the Specops blog, covered more than 260 million breached passwords from 2026. Specops told TNW they came from a mix of honeypots, infostealer logs and public breach dumps.

The research team searched for 26 holiday and seasonal terms. Together, they appeared more than 242,000 times. The counts are total occurrences, and they include predictable variations such as “Chr1sTmas” and “sN0w”, Specops said.

It has been revealed that after “santa” came “snow” (45,671) and “noel” (45,026). The short form “xmas” appeared 7,481 times, more than twice as often as the full word.

Month names were common too. “November” appeared 12,838 times and “december” 10,037 times, ahead of “advent” (8,722) and “merry” (4,378). Other Christmas words were far rarer: “rudolph” appeared 999 times, “reindeer” 371 and “mistletoe” 73. Shopping terms barely registered, with 195 uses of “blackfriday” and seven of “cybermonday”.

According to recent reports, specops notes that not every hit is a festive choice. “Snow”, “noel” and “november” all have meanings unrelated to the holidays.

Recent findings suggest that “Santa appearing more than 70,000 times might raise a smile, but it shows how often familiar words find their way into passwords. Holidays provide plenty of inspiration for people looking for something memorable, and attackers know it,” said Darren James, senior product manager at Specops Software, in a statement.

In a recent development, cracking tools test dictionaries of common words along with predictable tweaks, such as capital letters, swapped characters and numbers. Adding “123” or an exclamation mark can satisfy a complexity rule without making a password much harder to crack, the firm noted.

Every password in the study had already leaked, and Specops states that is the bigger risk. Attackers can use those passwords directly. In credential stuffing, they try stolen logins on other accounts where people have reused them.

According to recent reports, old credentials keep doing damage. Attackers cracked 75,000 Fortinet firewalls this year using old passwords, not a zero-day. Earlier this month, TNW reported that infostealers had reached 72% of firms.

Earlier in 2026, Specops found that 19% of passwords compromised in a single month met typical enterprise complexity requirements.

“A password can meet every complexity requirement and still put an organization at risk if it has already been compromised,” James stated.

Sources indicate that specops sells tools that block breached passwords in Active Directory. Alongside the research, it added more than 460 million compromised passwords to its Breached Password Protection database, which now holds more than 6.5 billion.

A separate list behind Password Auditor, the organization’s free audit tool, gained more than 4.6 million records and now holds more than 1.1 billion. TNW has reported that the passwordless future is still years away for most businesses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

It has been revealed that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session highlights how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

Recent findings suggest that in the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also demonstrates how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

It has been revealed that you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

In a recent development, what should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that consumers have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a newly introduced setting so people can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

Sources indicate that by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It has been revealed that it’s not exactly a “upcoming feature,” but iPhone Duo owners will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • In a recent development, GTA 6 is absurdly large.
  • Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

In a recent development, GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

According to recent reports, you can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Sources indicate that let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

Sources indicate that file size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

Sources indicate that according to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

Industry observers note that first, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Recent findings suggest that also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

Sources indicate that more importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

Industry observers note that the DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#39289. Industry News: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3526 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Sources indicate that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

According to recent reports, “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

According to recent reports, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Sources indicate that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Recent findings suggest that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team revealed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Industry observers note that remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

It has been revealed that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga indicates, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga claims. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

In a recent development, dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Fresh York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

Industry observers note that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

According to recent reports, remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In a recent development, in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics tech giant XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Sources indicate that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

In a recent development, nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Sources indicate that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

Recent findings suggest that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

It has been revealed that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, claims experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” states neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

According to recent reports, telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

According to recent reports, “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

It has been revealed that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Recent findings suggest that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as rapidly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy confirmed US $62 million in latest funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Recent findings suggest that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this newly introduced technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Recent findings suggest that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff presents the Dreamforce 2026 main keynote.
  • Salesforce’s consortium is one of 33 that the US Commerce Department has picked to sell American “Super Intelligence” technology abroad.
  • The programme carries out President Trump’s Executive Order 14320, on promoting the export of the American SI technology stack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff presents the Dreamforce 2026 main keynote.

Salesforce’s consortium is one of 33 that the US Commerce Department has picked to sell American “Super Intelligence” technology abroad. Commerce named the first group on Monday under its American SI Exports Program, and Salesforce confirmed its place on Thursday.

The programme carries out President Trump’s Executive Order 14320, on promoting the export of the American SI technology stack. Each consortium had to offer a package covering every layer: hardware, data pipelines and labelling, models, security, and applications.

US commercial diplomats will offer the packages to foreign governments and customers from a “menu”. Chosen packages get priority government-to-government engagement, faster export control reviews, and priority referrals for federal financing.

“The United States is the global leader in trusted SI research, development, and innovation,” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said in a statement.

A second, on-demand phase opens for applications on 30 November. It lets companies apply for single deals without offering the full stack. The scheme comes as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly set to be named AI national champions.

Industry observers note that salesforce’s package runs on Hyperforce, its cloud architecture on US infrastructure, with Informatica handling data governance. AI agents run on its own xGen models and third-party models, through the Agentforce platform.

According to recent reports, kendall Collins leads the bid. He runs Missionforce, Salesforce’s government cloud business. The company indicates its technology already supports government work in more than 30 countries and all 15 US Cabinet departments.

Industry observers note that the designation caps a crowded few days for the organization. On Monday, Salesforce told staff that every role now has a monthly AI token budget. Some employees had spent thousands of dollars a month on tokens, Business Insider reported from an internal memo.

“Starting this month, every role has a monthly token budget, so we can focus our AI spend on the work that matters most for our customers and business,” chief operating officer Miguel Milano wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the caps run from $100 a month for sellers to $1,000 for technical roles in sales. A Salesforce spokesperson told Business Insider the organization has no companywide individual budgets and leaves AI usage to team leaders. Apple cut its engineers’ AI budgets this month.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, Microsoft and Salesforce declared Copilotforce at Ignite, the same keynote where Microsoft said Copilot beats Claude on price. It brings Salesforce customer data and 38 prebuilt sales skills into Microsoft Copilot, in public preview.

Salesforce has also started cutting more jobs, Business Insider reported from internal messages. The scale of the cuts is unclear. Salesforce shares fell 9% on Tuesday, according to the same report.

#39285. Tech Report: I tested GPT-6.2 vs. Gemini 4 Hydrogen on 5 tasks — it wasn't even close

📖 Baca

Tech Report: I tested GPT-6.2 vs. Gemini 4 Hydrogen on 5 tasks — it wasn't even close

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google and OpenAI are going head-to-head again, and this time, their newest AI models arrived just five days apart.
  • It has been revealed that google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, promising faster responses, stronger reasoning and better performance across everyday tasks.
  • Both companies are making substantial promises about what their AI can do, but benchmarks and launch demos only tell part of the story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google and OpenAI are going head-to-head again, and this time, their newest AI models arrived just five days apart.

It has been revealed that google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, promising faster responses, stronger reasoning and better performance across everyday tasks. Then, on November 17, OpenAI fired back with GPT-6.2 Astra, its latest model designed to tackle everything from complex research and writing to coding and creative projects.

Both companies are making substantial promises about what their AI can do, but benchmarks and launch demos only tell part of the story. What matters is how these models perform when you actually put them to work.

So I put Gemini 4 Hydrogen and GPT-6.2 Astra through the same five real-world challenges to see which one delivers better results, where each struggles and which AI is actually worth using.

Prompt: You're an event coordinator managing a one-day technology conference with 120 attendees, three meeting rooms and six speakers.

The conference runs from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Each speaker must deliver one 45-minute presentation. Every presentation requires a 15-minute room reset afterward.

Speaker A is available only before noon.

Speaker B cannot present before 11 a.m.

Speakers C and D must not present at the same time.

Speaker E must present immediately after Speaker A, in the same room, allowing for the required room reset.

Speaker F is available only between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.

All attendees must have a shared lunch break from noon to 1 p.m.

Each room can host no more than three presentations.

A 30-minute keynote involving all six speakers must take place at 4:30 p.m.

Create a complete conference schedule showing start times, end times, room assignments and speakers. Identify any conflicts and explain how you resolved them. Do not change any constraints without explicitly stating why.

According to recent reports, GPT-6.2 identified both keynote conflicts, and it also identified the exceptions that would need approval. This directly addresses the instruction not to change constraints without explaining why. It correctly scheduled the six individual presentations and revealed reset periods explicitly and preserved the shared lunch break.

Hydrogen was strong on presentation and the mechanics of the individual talks. Its table is easy to follow, with resets alongside each presentation. It also correctly handles the A-to-E sequence, B’s earliest start, C and D’s separation, F’s individual talk, lunch, and room limits. It also explains why the selected times work for the individual presentations.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins on constraint reasoning and transparency. Hydrogen offers a solid schedule, but it mistakes fitting the individual presentations into the day for satisfying the entire conference specification.

It has been revealed that prompt: Write the opening 500 words of a literary mystery novel. A woman arrives at a small coastal town to attend the funeral of someone she has never met. Everyone in town recognizes her, but nobody will explain why.

Write in first person, past tense.

Start with a sentence of exactly seven words.

Include a conversation that sounds natural but contains a hidden threat.

Establish a distinctive setting without using a long descriptive paragraph.

Introduce one seemingly insignificant object that becomes important in the final sentence.

Do not use the words "mysterious," "secret," "shadow," or "dark.".

End with a revelation that changes how the reader understands the opening.

Industry observers note that avoid clichés, melodrama and obvious AI-generated prose. Prioritize believable characters and original storytelling.

In a recent development, GPT-6.2 delivered an opening sentence that satisfies the seven-word rule and it introduced the identity question without explaining it. The narrator feels like a believable person and the setting emerges through activity. The threatening conversation retains plausible deniability. Alan’s questions about whether anyone expects her back could be concern or an assessment of how easily she could disappear. “If you get a signal” sharpens that uncertainty. That said, the ending is overcompressed.Hydrogen provided a clear, accessible opening with an easy-to-follow progression from ferry to town to diner. Its opening sentence also contains exactly seven words: “The morning ferry docked at eleven sharp.” It maintains first-person, past-tense narration and avoids the prohibited words. Hydrogen’s main weakness is that the final revelation does not sufficiently change our understanding of the opening.

Industry observers note that winner: GPT-6.2 wins for an ending that makes the reader reconsider what already happened. Hydrogen’s ending mainly makes the reader wonder what happens next. Both can create suspense, but GPT-6.2 answers this prompt more successfully.

Prompt: Build a fully functional, interactive website called "Decision Lab" that helps people compare difficult choices.

People should be able to enter up to five options, define their own decision criteria, assign importance weights from 1 to 10, and score each option against every criterion.

Automatically calculate weighted scores and rank the options.

Display a visual chart comparing the results.

Let customers edit or delete options and criteria.

Include a sensitivity analysis showing whether the winner changes when the most important criterion's weight is reduced by 50%.

Include a "What if?" feature that lets people adjust weights and immediately see updated rankings.

Provide three realistic sample decisions that consumers can load instantly.

Save user changes between sessions if the environment supports persistent storage.

Recent findings suggest that use a modern, polished interface with intuitive controls. Every button and calculation must actually work.

In a recent development, don't create a static mockup. Build the functioning app, then test its calculations and interactions. Explain any limitations.

GPT-6.2 built and published an interactive website for comparing up to five choices. I simply enter what matters, give each criterion a weight, and score the options. The site ranks them and updates the chart as changes are made. It also added a “what if?” slider section to experiment without changing original weights.

Recent findings suggest that hydrogen built a self-contained, responsive web application and tested its calculations and controls before displaying it. It also build a scoring matrix, added support for up to 5 options and implemented live calculations and charting.

It has been revealed that winner: GPT-6.2 wins for a more thorough and useful website. The interactive site followed the prompt exactly while also adding extras that were useful for the overall project.

Prompt: You're the operations manager of an independent bookstore.

According to recent reports, it's 4 p.m. on Friday, and the following problems happen simultaneously:.

A bestselling author is arriving at 5 p.m. for a signing attended by 80 customers.

The shipment containing 60 copies of the author's book is delayed until Monday.

You have only 12 copies in stock.

Your only experienced employee just called in sick.

A customer claims they were charged twice for a $75 purchase, but your payment system is offline.

A local journalist is asking whether the store is experiencing financial difficulties.

Your landlord has emailed demanding an overdue $2,000 payment by Monday.

You have $900 in available business cash, two inexperienced employees and one hour before the event.

Develop a realistic action plan.

Rank problems by urgency, explain what you would do in the first 15 minutes, write a short statement for customers attending the signing, and draft a response to the journalist.

You cannot cancel the event, invent money, pretend books have arrived or promise refunds that you cannot verify.

In a recent development, be transparent without creating unnecessary panic. Explain what information you still need before making irreversible decisions.

In a recent development, GPT-6.2 treated the task as several connected operational problems, rather than simply a shortage of books. It prioritized safe event operations and gave inexperienced staff narrow roles. It checked capacity, kept exits clear, and assigned responsibility for the queue to better manage 80 attendees without the experienced employee.Hydrogen was practical in several aspects. But it promised to put bookplates into books “as soon as the boxes arrive Monday.” That turns the expected shipment date into a firm fulfillment commitment. Overall, the model introduced several unsupported assumptions — and its customer statement promises arrangements that its own strategy says still need confirmation.

In a recent development, winner: GPT-6.2 wins as the stronger operations-manager answer because it preserved options while keeping customers, staff, the author and the landlord informed. Hydrogen had useful ideas but repeatedly moved from “ask whether this is possible” to “tell customers this will happen.”.

Prompt: Five researchers, Ava, Ben, Chloe, Daniel and Elena, each work on a different project (robotics, climate, medicine, astronomy and cybersecurity), use a different programming language (Python, Rust, JavaScript, Go and Julia), and work on a different floor (1 through 5).

Determine each researcher's project, programming language and floor using these clues:.

The robotics researcher works on floor 5.

The person using Rust works exactly one floor above the climate researcher.

Ben works on a lower floor than Chloe.

The astronomy researcher uses Julia.

The cybersecurity researcher works on floor 1.

Elena works exactly two floors below the robotics researcher.

The medicine researcher uses Python.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

It has been revealed that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Industry observers note that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”.

The only things in that list which should ever be leaving my device are “deep research” (clearly asking online repositories) and "summarizing photo content.” Everything else has no reason not to be done on device, and as such can’t have any limits.

But leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”.

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”.

It would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for customers. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

“It’s actually about earning the right to be a part of the conversation that is the most influential conversation in making a purchase decision.” Ronan Harris, Snap.

In a recent development, harris became Snap’s Chief Commercial Officer two months ago, after nearly four years leading its European business. Before that he spent 17 years at Google.

Industry observers note that he spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at Web Summit in Lisbon on 12 November. He had spoken at the very first Web Summit, when he ran Google in Ireland. Earlier episodes featured Kristin Fracchia of Gamma, Jim Lanzone of Yahoo, and Alexander Rinke of Celonis. The full conversation is in the video below.

Sources indicate that snap makes money in two main ways, Harris stated: advertising, and a growing in-app business of subscriptions and digital products. Snapchat is approaching a billion people a month, and engaged users open it 40 or 50 times a day, he said.

The app opens to the camera, which has become a way to communicate. Chat is where people spend most of their time. The map is for exploring and organising their lives, and a content section is for creators and discovery. Advertisers can connect into each of those.

Sources indicate that harris called the idea that Snapchat is for teenagers a misconception. One in four owners is 35 or older, he remarked, and 80% are 18 or older. In France, the average age on the platform is 35. In the Nordics and the Middle East, Snapchat is the primary platform for all ages, he said.

“We are the internet’s best-kept secret at the moment when it comes to ad results.” Ronan Harris, Snap.

It has been revealed that snap’s lenses for Walmart, which bring the retailer’s product catalogue to life in augmented reality, have had more than 160 million engagements, Harris said. They send people to the website or, through the map and Snap’s Promoted Places product, to a store. A Gucci campaign reached 7.7 million Snapchatters, who spent on average 11 seconds using the lenses.

A fresh format, Sponsored Snaps, puts brands alongside the chats people have with friends and family. Snap is the first platform to do this, Harris said. According to Snap, 61% of Snapchatters say friends and family are their most influential source for purchase decisions.

He cited research by Mindscope, a behavioural research tech giant. It found that consumers are moving away from traditional social media and into private spaces. His advice to marketers is to initiative for where consumers will be in 2027, and to earn their participation instead of chasing reach.

It has been revealed that four years ago, Snap was harder to buy than the major platforms, Harris said. It was easier for advertisers to keep spending with them.

“Nobody’s gonna get fired for buying a little bit more Google.” Ronan Harris, Snap.

Conversions that Snap delivers for app advertisers have doubled year over year, while the cost per conversion fell by about 24%, he remarked. Direct response advertising, which Snap did not have when he joined, is now the largest part of its business. His pitch is to move the least-performing 5% or 10% of a budget to Snap and test it.

It has been revealed that AI works in the background, he remarked, powering ad products and lenses. Dynamic product generative retrieval and agentic recommendations have brought a step change in pixel purchases on the platform.

Recent findings suggest that harris studied electronic engineering and spent 10 years in Japan. After consulting, a security and authentication startup and some time in private equity, he joined Google in early 2005.

Google had nearly 2,000 people worldwide then, and about 25 in Dublin, he noted. He stayed in Dublin for 11 years and spent his last six years at Google running the UK and Ireland business from London. He moved to Snap, he said, to play where the community was going.
