Fig and Elastic partner to help security teams prevent silent gaps in detection coverage

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Fig Security graphic marking its partnership with Elastic.
  • In a recent development, security teams rely on detection rules to identify suspicious activity across increasingly complex technology environments.
  • Recent findings suggest that addressing this challenge, Fig has confirmed an integration partnership with Elastic designed to help security teams maintain detection coverage as their environments evolve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Fig Security graphic marking its partnership with Elastic.

In a recent development, security teams rely on detection rules to identify suspicious activity across increasingly complex technology environments. But even when those rules remain active, changes to the underlying data can quietly undermine their effectiveness. A vendor updating its log format, a new data source entering the environment or a pipeline modification can leave detection logic without the information it needs to identify threats.

Recent findings suggest that addressing this challenge, Fig has confirmed an integration partnership with Elastic designed to help security teams maintain detection coverage as their environments evolve. The integration combines Elastic Security’s open, agentic security operations platform with Fig’s capabilities for mapping detection dependencies, identifying breaks and validating changes before they reach production.

The partnership aims to give security operations teams greater visibility into the relationship between their data infrastructure and the detection rules that depend on it.

Detection engineering involves more than creating rules that identify suspicious behavior. Those rules depend on data arriving in specific structures, containing particular fields and values that allow security teams to recognize potentially malicious activity.

When those dependencies change, detection coverage can deteriorate without producing an obvious warning. Data may continue flowing, and detection rules may remain enabled, even though the information required to identify an attack is no longer available.

In a recent development, these changes are not necessarily caused by mistakes. Organizations regularly modify their data pipelines to improve performance, introduce upcoming vendors or accommodate evolving infrastructure requirements. However, changes made outside security teams’ direct control can have downstream consequences for detection engineering.

Recent findings suggest that this is where Fig’s integration with Elastic is designed to help. Rather than treating data infrastructure and detection rules as separate components, the integration connects changes upstream to the detections that depend on them.

According to recent reports, fig connects to an Elastic environment through a read-only API key and retrieves its configuration. Its deterministic Security Data Lineage then maps the relationships between data sources, pipelines, mappings, fields and detection rules.

Industry observers note that this creates a dependency map that allows engineers to understand what each detection rule requires before making changes to the environment. When a source, pipeline or mapping changes, Fig identifies the affected detections and pinpoints where the data flow has broken.

The platform also recommends fixes, giving engineers information they can use to investigate the underlying glitch and evaluate potential repairs.

For Gal Shafir, Co-Founder and CEO of Fig, the partnership addresses two complementary areas of security engineering.

Recent findings suggest that “Elastic gives security teams control over their data, and Fig gives them control over the engineering around it,” said Shafir. “Teams can see how every source connects to every detection, test each change against their own environment and ship it as code. That lets them move rapidly without losing sight of their coverage.”.

The distinction is notable as organizations introduce latest data sources and continuously adjust the infrastructure supporting their security operations.

In a recent development, elastic provides prebuilt integrations and research-backed detection rules to help organizations establish security coverage from the beginning. Its Automatic Import and AI Agent capabilities also help teams develop newly introduced integrations and custom rules as their requirements expand.

Fig complements these capabilities by allowing engineers to test changes against their organization’s actual data and environment context before deploying them.

Once changes have been validated, teams can ship them as code through continuous integration and continuous delivery workflows. Version control and one-click rollback provide additional control over deployment.

Jamie Hynds, Director of Product at Elastic, highlighted the importance of maintaining visibility as security environments change.

Industry observers note that “Environments never stop changing, from vendor schemas and APIs to ETL tools and pipelines. Fig traces those changes to the detection rules that depend on them, so SecOps teams can adapt promptly and maintain detection coverage with Elastic Security,” noted Hynds.

Sources indicate that the integration also addresses organizations migrating from another security information and event management platform. Elastic’s Automatic Migration translates existing detection rules, while Fig checks those translated rules against the data available in Elastic before cutover.

The process identifies rules that require rework and recommends fixes, helping engineering teams align detection logic with the destination environment before completing the transition.

The Fig and Elastic integration is now available. Security teams can book a demonstration through fig.security to see how Fig maps their Elastic environment.

In a recent development, as security environments continue to evolve, maintaining effective detection coverage requires more than keeping rules active. It also requires understanding the data dependencies behind them and validating changes before they affect production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

The latest version of the following popular software bundles an affected Ruby.

Updated 19 November 2026 at 14:29 UTC.

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

Sources indicate that install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

In a recent development, most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

Recent findings suggest that the output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

Recent findings suggest that the same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

In a recent development, A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

We'll be publishing a proof of concept in a week, once people have had time to upgrade.

#39269. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple responds]

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1130 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple responds]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable people to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow owners to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable people to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow owners to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed owners to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

It has been revealed that A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta stated they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, noted that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Sources indicate that update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple stated:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the tech giant noted does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

It has been revealed that as for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Sources indicate that look, my last name is literally England. If I can’t stop my fellow Brits from getting rinsed by fake Black Friday laptop deals, I might as well hand in my passport and never go to a chippy again.

It has been revealed that you already know the name of the game — U.K. tech retail is a minefield because the memory shortage jacked up the launch prices of almost every new notebook this year.

Every discount screams about a “massive Black Friday saving,” but it’s artificially bloated.

Every Black Friday computing deal we recommend passes two rigorous tests to ensure it is cheaper than its original RRP before the memory crisis began. That's the 'RAMageddon Reset' promise.

In a recent development, and that’s why I’m activating my personal BS detector with the RAMageddon Reset rules. I dug through Amazon and Currys' sales to find the laptops that actually pass the sniff test, and are at a lower price than the RRP from before this memory surge.

Asus Zenbook 14 (Snapdragon X, 16GB).

HP OmniBook 5 16" OLED (Snapdragon X, 16GB).

Microsoft Surface Laptop 8 (Snapdragon X2 Plus).

HP OmniBook 5 16" LCD (24GB RAM).

Asus Chromebook Plus CX1405 (8GB RAM).

Snapdragon X1 ⏐ 16GB RAM ⏐ 256GB SSD.

In a recent development, much more bang for your buck than the MacBook Neo (which is actually more money), the Zenbook 14 is quite the performer with Snapdragon X and 16GB of RAM on-board. Take the inflated RRP out of the equation and look at the pre-crisis RRP of a similar system (£650), this is bang on the retail price you’d expect to pay.

Apple M5 | 16GB RAM | 512GB SSD.

Recent findings suggest that when the M5 Air came out, Apple baked a £100 AI-era tax into its price, so I ignored £1,499 and looked at the pre-crisis M4 Air 15-inch — which launched at £1,399. You’re beating last year’s RRP by £100 on one of the best ultraportable big screen notebooks that money can buy.

Snapdragon X | 16GB RAM | 256GB SSD.

Industry observers note that even when you ignore that inflated £1,199 RRP (original UK price for this option is £849), at £599, this OLED looker is quite a steal! With that 16-inch 2K panel, Snapdragon X zippiness and 16GB of RAM, this is a well-featured machine that Currys tried to sneak into their sale quietly.

Snapdragon X2 Plus | 16GB RAM | 512GB SSD.

With a mid-2026 Snapdragon X2 Plus chip in here, I compared this price to the RRP of the pre-crisis Surface Laptop 7 with the Snapdragon X Plus. This debuted at £1,249, so you’re getting a deal that undercuts pre-shortage launch pricing by 28%. Plus, it’s a rather premium notebook as you can read in our review.

AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 | 24GB RAM | 1TB SSD.

This sneaky deal gives you 24GB of RAM inside the nicely premium OmniBook 5 for less than the pre-crisis 16GB model’s £929 RRP. It’s a simple utilitarian workhorse with plenty of mid-range performance for getting stuff done, as well as that additional memory headroom. The main difference between this and the other OmniBook is that it has an LCD display.

Intel Core 3 N355 | 8GB RAM | 256GB SSD.

Industry observers note that this passes both my tests by dipping well under that pre-RAMageddon baseline RRP of £399. And while Windows 11 is dealing with 8GB of RAM better, it still runs a little chunky. ChromeOS runs effortlessly on what is a sleek notebook for basic browsing and students.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its owners’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let owners edit a Story after publishing.

This means people will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that customers will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s revision is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

It has been revealed that back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (420 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Google’s Gemini 4 Neon ranks third in AI tests, replacing Argon in Gemini

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (420 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a model that sits between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon in its line-up.
  • Neon is Google’s fourth Gemini 4 model since Argon arrived on 30 September.
  • “Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently,” Kavukcuoglu wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a model that sits between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon in its line-up. It is rolling out now in the Gemini API, Gemini for business, Google Antigravity and the Gemini app. Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP of Google DeepMind and Google’s chief AI architect, confirmed it in a blog post on Wednesday.

Neon is Google’s fourth Gemini 4 model since Argon arrived on 30 September. It follows Gemini 4 Carbon on 10 November and Gemini 4 Hydrogen two days later.

“Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently,” Kavukcuoglu wrote.

Neon costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15. It has a 1 million-token context window and four thinking levels: low, medium, high (the default) and xhigh.

Google indicates Neon scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at xhigh, third overall. Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking firm, put it behind OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2. It sits one point ahead of Carbon.

The firm also showed where the savings come from. Neon used about 15% more output tokens per task than Carbon. Its lower cost per task, $6.44 against $7.76, comes from cheaper tokens, not shorter answers. It also ran at about 110 output tokens per second, against about 57 for Carbon.

On coding agents, the firm scored Neon at 59. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 both scored 58. Neon cost $6.86 per task, against $12.61 for Opus and $15.47 for Fable.

Those cost figures use Carbon’s standard price of $4 and $20. Until 30 November, Carbon sells at an introductory $2 and $10, which leaves Neon 50% dearer for now, Artificial Analysis noted.

In Antigravity, Neon can also direct parallel Hydrogen subagents as an orchestrator, Google mentioned.

A cyber version of Neon will reach eligible defenders over the next few days. It goes through Google’s Fairwind Program, the route that gave cyber defenders Argon first.

Google says Neon scored 90.5% on SEC-bench Pro, a test of finding code flaws. It did so at about half the cost per challenge of rivals. It also says Neon keeps Carbon’s safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse, while turning down far fewer legitimate tasks in those areas.

3 fresh to Netflix thriller movies you should stream this week — including the No. 1 film in the top 10 right now, and a '90s Harrison Ford action classic (Nov. 19-26)

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're looking to find the best thriller movies to watch on Netflix this week, then you're in the right place.
  • This week's selection kicks off with a upcoming Indonesian thriller that has taken the world by storm.
  • Sources indicate that all three of these films deliver their fair share of action, surprises, suspense, and drama and are ideal for spreading out across the week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're looking to find the best thriller movies to watch on Netflix this week, then you're in the right place. I've scoured the list of all the fresh movies that are arriving on the streamer this month and hand-picked three that I'll be adding to my watchlist.

This week's selection kicks off with a upcoming Indonesian thriller that has taken the world by storm. We're following that up with a '90s action classic starring Harrison Ford. Then, finally, we're bringing it all home with a cult favorite in which Sylvester Stallone takes on the elements as well as gun-totting criminals. Can you guess which blockbuster we're talking about?

Sources indicate that all three of these films deliver their fair share of action, surprises, suspense, and drama and are ideal for spreading out across the week. So, without further ado, let's take a look at the best Netflix thriller movies to watch this week.

According to recent reports, this Indonesian action thriller has surprised everyone by becoming the No. 1 most-streamed movie on Netflix this week, charting in 89 regions around the world. It follows Hari (Lukman Sardi), a retired soldier haunted by the past and has retreated to a quiet life in the countryside. His isolation is broken when his son highlights up and asks him to look after his two grandchildren. If that wasn't bad enough, it's at this exact moment that a crime syndicate chooses to come after Hari for revenge, forcing him to fall back on his military training to survive.

According to recent reports, directed by Sidharta Tata, "Never Surrender" transcends its — let's be honest — pretty predictable plot thanks to some excellent fight choreography, interspersed with heartfelt bonding between Hari and the two kids, Dimas (Sultan Hamonangan) and Putri (Callista Arum). If that sounds cheesy, then, yeah, it is a bit, but the cast are likeable and the action scenes exciting enough to make this more than worth your time.

Watch "Never Surrender" on Netflix now.

In a recent development, wolfgang Petersen's 1997 action classic delivers a stirring role for Harrison Ford as James Marshall, an ass-kicking Commander-in-Chief, who is called on to save the day when the presidential plane is hijacked by Russian terrorists. Leading the baddies is Gary Oldman, in fine snarling form as Egor Kurshonov (Gary Oldman) who threatens to kill everybody onboard unless terrorist leader General Radek (Jürgen Prochnow) is released from prison. Marshall fakes his escape and then does a "Die Hard": taking out the baddies one-by-one as he tries to stop Kurshonov and free his captured family.

"Air Force One" was released in the same year as another beloved plane-based thriller, "Con Air". The two movies are quite different, however, with "Air Force One" delivering a more straight-down-the-line action movie than the Nicolas Cage-starring caper. Wolfgang Petersen is a master of taut thrills, as anyone who has seen his submarine-based masterpiece "Das Boot" can attest. "Air Force One" isn't quite that good, but it's a rollicking good time all the same.

Watch "Air Force One" on Netflix.

It's fair to say that this Sylvester Stallone-starring survival thriller met with a mixed response when it premiered in 1993, with the legendary critic Gene Siskel describing the film as being "filled with howlingly bad scenes." He was not alone in that opinion. Over the years, however, "Cliffhanger" has become something of a cult classic – enough so that a remake is on the cards for early 2027.

Ably helmed by "Die Hard 2" director Renny Harlin, "Cliffhanger" follows rescue ranger Gabe Walker (Stallone), recently traumatized by the death of a friend in a mountaineering accident. Walker quits, but agrees to take on one last job: helping rescue the survivors of a plane crash, little realizing that they are actually deadly mercenaries, led by the psychotic Eric Qualen (John Lithgow).

Sources indicate that cue lots of jumping, swinging, and hanging vertiginously as the inaptly named Walker saves the day. Yes, "Cliffhanger" is silly, but it's also a huge amount of fun — and sometimes that's exactly what you want from a thriller.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month.
  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

Industry observers note that when we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a significant way on latest and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

Sources indicate that the really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are latest or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very notable to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a newly introduced logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe stated he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The glitch of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

According to recent reports, well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a tech giant and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s Voyager building at its headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
  • Nvidia spent $58.1bn buying shares in other companies in the nine months to 25 October.
  • Recent findings suggest that the investments focus on “frontier labs, infrastructure financiers, and other private companies”, according to Nvidia’s CFO commentary, Fortune reported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s Voyager building at its headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Nvidia spent $58.1bn buying shares in other companies in the nine months to 25 October. That is almost 12 times the $4.95bn of a year earlier. Fortune found the figure in the quarterly results Nvidia posted on Tuesday. It nearly matches the $61.2bn Nvidia spent buying back its own stock, up from $36.3bn.

Recent findings suggest that the investments focus on “frontier labs, infrastructure financiers, and other private companies”, according to Nvidia’s CFO commentary, Fortune reported. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI and Anthropic.

Fortune noted that this raises the question of circular financing: whether Nvidia is funding the demand that drives its own sales. The IMF warned last month that such deals could deepen a market correction. If AI spending slows, Nvidia could lose twice: through weaker chip sales and through falling values for its stakes. James Kisner, managing director of technology at Water Tower Research, made that point to Fortune.

“It’s magnified and you feel more pain because you’re kind of double exposed here,” Kisner said.

The stakes produced $1.8bn of net gains in the quarter, Fortune reported. That figure includes a $1bn loss on its private holdings.

Nvidia’s backing goes beyond shares. Neoclouds are firms that rent out computing power on Nvidia chips. On the earnings call, interim chief executive Colette Kress stated Nvidia’s future commitments to them totalled $32bn in the quarter. Its credit guarantees reached $118bn. That includes $105bn for the PORTS-Pike data centre in Ohio, which OpenAI will lease for 20 years.

Some of those guarantees only start once a customer has financing in place, Kress remarked.

“If all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” she mentioned.

According to recent reports, kress called shareholder returns a “super top priority”. Nvidia has $227.3bn left under its buyback programme and plans to use it by the end of fiscal 2028, she mentioned. She also told analysts on Tuesday that Nvidia was rigorously evaluating future investments and guarantees.

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

In a recent development, data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

Industry observers note that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” indicates Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Industry observers note that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” states Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Upcoming Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Sources indicate that inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Recent findings suggest that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon indicates this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How massive do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also vital to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is presently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In a recent development, with AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.

According to recent reports, taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the manufacturer’s tech to beat GPUs.

Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr indicates.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

Recent findings suggest that the Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

Recent findings suggest that the startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

Industry observers note that the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen indicates, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is presently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr indicates. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

It has been revealed that free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another massive advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

It has been revealed that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

According to recent reports, “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

According to recent reports, one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

According to recent reports, the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main problem is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch claims, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

In a recent development, not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” notes Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the organization believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

Industry observers note that the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” claims Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the tech giant’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to rapidly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

According to recent reports, lightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the organization’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi claims. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

According to recent reports, yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

In a recent development, the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis.

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

It has been revealed that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

According to recent reports, new claims that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

Industry observers note that how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he states. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

Sources indicate that however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. States Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

Wall Street rallied into the debut. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.5% just after the 9:30am ET open, and the S&P 500 gained 1%, CNBC reported.

Sources indicate that perpetual futures pointed to a 25% gain on the $83 Anthropic IPO price, according to CNBC. Earlier, grey markets implied about 27%. Before the open, Alphabet rose 4.1%, Amazon 2.4% and Broadcom 2.9%. Amazon owns nearly 15% of Anthropic and Google about 14%, Bloomberg reported.

“It’ll be an key barometer for investors’ AI appetite,” Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp, told CNBC.

Cox also warned that hot IPOs rarely perform well straight out of the gate.

Analysts at firms outside the deal have started coverage. Needham rated the stock a buy, with a $150 price target. Across five buy ratings, the average target is about $116, according to Bloomberg’s data. Seaport Global’s Jay Goldberg started coverage without a rating or a target.

Growth is the question for some investors, Bloomberg’s Rebecca Torrence reported. Anthropic’s revenue reached $16.3bn in the first half of 2026, up about 1,300% on a year earlier. Third-quarter revenue grew 47% on the second quarter, down from 144% the quarter before.

Industry observers note that the bills are large too, after compute costs rose to 58% of revenue last quarter. Anthropic has signed about $900bn of compute deals, according to its filings. Nearly $71bn falls due in the next 12 months, Business Insider reported.

Recent findings suggest that current and former employees can sell up to 10% of their shares on IPO day, BI’s Stephen Council reported. Another 35% frees up early next year. After that, every employee must sell on fixed, pre-planned schedules, a rule most companies apply only to executives.

Some are already planning where the money goes. Current and former Anthropic staff have asked lawyers and family office consultants about setting up their own investment firms, CNBC’s Hayley Cuccinello reported. Altss, a private markets data firm, expects 15 to 20 new single-family offices from Anthropic wealth over three years.

“Don’t build the Taj Mahal of family office structures when you may have years potentially to realize the position,” consultant Kirby Rosplock told CNBC.

In a recent development, demand reaches beyond the US. Chinese retail investors want in despite steep pricing and regulatory barriers, the South China Morning Post reported. A 28-year-old consultant in Hangzhou told the paper the price was too high, but she would still buy a small amount.

Protesters unfurled banners outside the Nasdaq in Times Square at 9am, calling to “stop tech oligarchs” and “freeze AI”, BI reported.

Doubts also come from inside. One former employee, who left before the IPO, told The Verge’s Hayden Field the current pace of AI development feels “untenable under normal market structures”. On Wednesday, scientists and tech figures signed the MisAnthropic Statement, which says Anthropic is not a safe AI tech giant.

Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krthr

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work.
  • If you've never made one, the fold is simple.
  • I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work.

If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue.

I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes.

According to recent reports, the part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down:.

I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a fresh zine, so I built fanzines.app.

Industry observers note that in the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server.

Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine.

In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover.

Industry observers note that it looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left.

The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order.

I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it.

Sources indicate that when I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them.

Industry observers note that I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs (X, Y, Width, Height). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection.

The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text.

According to recent reports, before downloading the PDF, a Review step indicates the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact.

A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish. Changing the language keeps your current pages.

You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jared Sine, GoDaddy’s chief strategy and legal officer.
  • Sources indicate that AI agents need a shared way to check who they are dealing with, GoDaddy’s chief strategy and legal officer Jared Sine wrote in a Fortune op-ed on Thursday.
  • Sine’s answer is the Agent Name Service (ANS), an open standard that ties AI agents to internet domain names.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jared Sine, GoDaddy’s chief strategy and legal officer.

Sources indicate that AI agents need a shared way to check who they are dealing with, GoDaddy’s chief strategy and legal officer Jared Sine wrote in a Fortune op-ed on Thursday. Without one, he argued, the agent economy risks splitting into closed platforms and attracting fraud.

Sine’s answer is the Agent Name Service (ANS), an open standard that ties AI agents to internet domain names. GoDaddy built ANS and handed it to the Linux Foundation, which released it as a Linux Foundation project on 10 November. Sine discloses GoDaddy’s role in the piece.

Sine compared the problem to the early internet. The Domain Name System (DNS) turned hard-to-read server addresses into names like Amazon.com that customers could trust. AI agents now need something similar, he wrote.

Sources indicate that for example, a travel agent bot must be sure it is booking with a real airline, not a fake site. A shopping agent needs to check that the shop and payment provider are genuine before it buys.

Sine also warned of quieter risks. A supplier could buy a company’s procurement agent, keep its name and nudge it to favour its own products. ANS would let businesses check who runs an agent and whether its owner or software has changed, he wrote.

ANS has backing from companies including Cisco, Cloudflare and Salesforce. However, the approach has critics. The New Stack noted that it relies on DNS’s old trust model and is being pushed hardest by domain registrars, which stand to profit.

Recent findings suggest that in the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:.

I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

...until recently (October 2026):.

This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit.

The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

Industry observers note that these were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

Sources indicate that my router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”.

The devices have their own web interface:.

According to recent reports, when I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:.

The script runs at night checking for an open door:.

The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request: "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you.".

Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:.

After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.
