  • Ferrari has built a highly profitable business by deliberately limiting production, preserving brand exclusivity, and commanding premium prices.
  • While Rivian is growing revenue nearly twice as fast as Ferrari, their contrasting approaches to growth, profitability, and capital investment could have significant implications for shareholder returns heading into 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By RJ Fulton – Updated Nov 19, 2026 at 5:45AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Ferrari ›.

In a recent development, revenue growth is often a key consideration when evaluating stocks, but it doesn't always tell the full story. For investors comparing Ferrari (RACE -0.64%) and Rivian Automotive (RIVN +0.85%), the distinction between growth potential and established profitability is particularly crucial.

Ferrari has built a highly profitable business by deliberately limiting production, preserving brand exclusivity, and commanding premium prices. Rivian, meanwhile, is focused on expanding production, developing more affordable electric vehicles, and capturing a greater share of the commercial fleet market.

While Rivian is growing revenue nearly twice as fast as Ferrari, their contrasting approaches to growth, profitability, and capital investment could have significant implications for shareholder returns heading into 2027.

In a recent development, ferrari's competitive advantage stems from its ability to command premium prices while deliberately limiting production. By maintaining the exclusivity of its vehicles, Ferrari creates a degree of pricing power that few automotive manufacturers can replicate. The company also generates revenue through sponsorships, merchandise, and brand licensing, extending its business beyond traditional vehicle sales.

Industry observers note that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $8.2 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 5.7%. Ferrari generated $1.8 billion in net income over the same period, translating to an impressive profit margin of roughly 22%. Rather than relying on higher production volumes to drive growth, Ferrari can increase revenue through premium vehicle offerings, customization, and higher selling prices.

As of December 2025, Ferrari maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.7 and a current ratio of 2.0, indicating a relatively healthy balance sheet. Additionally, the company generated approximately $2 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2025. Ferrari's strong cash generation provides the financial flexibility to invest in latest vehicle technologies, return capital to shareholders, and preserve its competitive position without sacrificing profitability.

In a recent development, rivian is pursuing a considerably different growth strategy, focusing on scaling production of electric trucks, SUVs, and commercial delivery vans. Its relationship with Amazon (AMZN +1.56%), both a major customer and a shareholder, provides an established source of demand for commercial vehicles. Additionally, its joint venture with Volkswagen (VWAGY +0.28%) creates opportunities to monetize its vehicle software and electrical architecture beyond its own automotive business.

In a recent development, in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $6.5 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 11.1%. Despite growing revenue nearly twice as fast as Ferrari, Rivian recorded a net loss of approximately $3 billion, translating to a negative profit margin of roughly 46.2%. Achieving profitability will largely depend on Rivian's ability to reduce manufacturing costs and expand production, particularly through its more affordable R2 vehicle platform.

As of December 2025, Rivian maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.5 and a current ratio of 2.3. Although the latter suggests adequate short-term liquidity, the manufacturer recorded negative free cash flow of approximately $2.5 billion during fiscal 2025. While substantial capital investment is expected at this stage of Rivian's development, its continued cash burn raises questions about how much additional financing the company may require before achieving sustainable profitability.

One of Ferrari's primary risks is preserving the brand exclusivity that underpins its pricing power and exceptional profit margins. Expanding production too aggressively could undermine the scarcity that makes its vehicles so desirable. Ferrari must also navigate the transition toward electrification without alienating customers who value the performance, sound, and driving experience of its traditional combustion engines. Additionally, a prolonged economic downturn could weaken discretionary spending, even among its affluent customer base.

Recent findings suggest that rivian faces considerably greater financial and operational risks. The company must accelerate production and reduce manufacturing costs while maintaining competitive vehicle pricing. Its more affordable R2 platform will be particularly key in determining whether Rivian can attract a broader customer base and progress toward profitability. It also faces intense competition from established manufacturers like Ford Motor Company (F +0.53%) and General Motors (GM +0.77%), as well as potential supply chain disruptions related to battery materials and geopolitical tensions.

Ferrari trades at a significant premium based on its Forward P/E, which compares its price to future earnings estimates, while Rivian looks cheaper relative to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Ferrari trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 37.5, while Rivian lacks a meaningful forward earnings multiple because analysts expect the company to remain unprofitable. Ferrari also trades at 8.6 times sales, more than three times Rivian's multiple of 2.7. Although Rivian appears considerably cheaper relative to revenue, that discount reflects the uncertainty surrounding its path to profitability.

Sources indicate that heading into 2027, I would favor Ferrari. Its competitive advantage lies in its ability to grow revenue without significantly increasing production. Its affluent customer base, brand exclusivity, and exceptional pricing power provide a degree of protection against the price competition and margin pressures facing the broader automotive industry.

Rivian's R2 platform could substantially expand its customer base by making its vehicles more accessible to everyday consumers. However, translating faster revenue growth into sustainable profitability remains a considerable challenge, particularly amid elevated borrowing costs and intensifying competition in the electric vehicle market.

Sources indicate that while Ferrari's premium valuation leaves less room for disappointment, I believe its established profitability, strong cash generation, and durable competitive advantages justify paying a higher multiple. Rivian may offer greater upside if it successfully scales production and achieves profitability, but Ferrari offers a more attractive balance of risk and potential return heading into 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A newly identified vulnerability in Oracle Java could give hackers unauthorized access to major applications and allow them to run code without logging in.
  • “Roughly 90% of Fortune 500 companies run on Java,” Thai Duong, CEO of cybersecurity firm Calif, noted.
  • The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (and dubbed Java4Shell), corrupts memory when Java decodes Base64, a standard format used to transmit login credentials and file uploads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A newly identified vulnerability in Oracle Java could give hackers unauthorized access to major applications and allow them to run code without logging in. The flaw could affect a sweeping array of significant businesses, including tech companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and Netflix, which rely heavily on Java’s server-side software and core products.

“Roughly 90% of Fortune 500 companies run on Java,” Thai Duong, CEO of cybersecurity firm Calif, noted.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (and dubbed Java4Shell), corrupts memory when Java decodes Base64, a standard format used to transmit login credentials and file uploads.

Duong told CNET that his manufacturer identified the critical software vulnerability in October and notified Oracle, which has since patched the vulnerability. This week, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued guidance urging organizations to do the same immediately. CISA recommends identifying affected Java installations, reviewing software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, and applying vendor patches as soon as they’re available.

Oracle rated the flaw a serious 8.1 out of 10 on the standard vulnerability scale. It can lead to an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Java, allowing hackers to run their own malicious commands or code over the internet without requiring a username, password or prior access.

Federico Kirschbaum, head of Security Lab, the research arm at cybersecurity company Xbow, told CNET that Java is primarily used at the enterprise level. As a result, the vulnerability could trickle across different sectors, including finance, government, transportation and large corporations.

“Java is a great language for creating solutions, but this vulnerability — it’s a reminder that maybe the languages that we’re using have flaws, and everything built on those might inherit that problem,” Kirschbaum stated.

Amid recent technological disruptions, he suggested leaning on AI solutions to address vulnerabilities in AI.

“That new normal is that most of the technology we rely on has flaws, and now that we have resources using LLMs, we can find those problems,” Kirschbaum noted.

He pointed out that bad actors and hackers can also find these vulnerabilities.

“We are in a race to find the problems first and help the industry by guiding them on what’s urgent so they patch it,” Kirschbaum noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that states “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.).

Sources indicate that A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get customers familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other consumers. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s fresh Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours.

It has been revealed that when a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and enhancement in real time, Google indicates. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the fresh feature more comparable.

#39180. Voyager 1 Becomes the First Spacecraft to Travel a Full Light-Day From Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager 1 Becomes the First Spacecraft to Travel a Full Light-Day From Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NASA’s Voyager 1 left Earth on Sept.
  • It has been revealed that at 5:16:07 a.m.
  • NASA puts the journey at 49 years, two months and 11 days, counting from Voyager 1’s launch in September 1977.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA’s Voyager 1 left Earth on Sept. 5, 1977, carrying a camera, a set of science instruments and a gold-plated record of sounds and images from home. Forty-nine years later, it’s reached a distance no spacecraft has attained before: one light-day, or roughly 16.1 billion miles, from Earth. At that range, light needs a full 24 hours to make the trip between Earth and the probe.

It has been revealed that at 5:16:07 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to reach that light-day milestone. From that point on, a radio signal between the spacecraft and NASA’s Deep Space Network takes more than a day to travel in either direction.

NASA puts the journey at 49 years, two months and 11 days, counting from Voyager 1’s launch in September 1977. The probe still sends data home, though at a rate slower than dial-up, and NASA plans a live discussion with the Voyager team on Thursday to mark the occasion.

According to recent reports, it’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s. One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to travel that distance on foot.

It has been revealed that fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster. It at the moment zips through the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after the spacecraft passed Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

According to recent reports, NASA marked the milestone with a global Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day event on Tuesday evening. Just after sunset, the agency wanted people to head outside and point their smartphone or tablet lights skyward to spark a planet-wide wave of light as Earth rotates, much like fans doing the wave at a stadium.

The space agency also made a website for the occasion. The website is simple. It flashes Voyager’s VGR call sign in Morse code. If you want to try it, click the link, hit begin, and then point your phone or tablet screen at the sky. The website does all the work for you.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory will follow up on Thursday at noon ET with a moderated discussion on the milestone, featuring status updates on both Voyager probes and a live Q&A with reporters and audience members.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the spacecraft’s life. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance, and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s lifespan.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called the Major Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

According to recent reports, it was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for a signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

Industry observers note that all of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two operational instruments.

Sources indicate that making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

Industry observers note that when Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, those generators now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

According to recent reports, the same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually introduced 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks.
  • Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model reveals 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.
  • Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model reveals 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

It has been revealed that microsoft indicates MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also crucial to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Industry observers note that throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex.

Sources indicate that one thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the tech giant’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As customers adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous.

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

According to recent reports, this becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the organization itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

It has been revealed that let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a firm is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these upcoming models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

According to recent reports, also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first.

A organization with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

Recent findings suggest that A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft indicates the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Recent findings suggest that benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the fresh models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open problem.

Recent findings suggest that the firm also described clearly that these upcoming models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these upcoming models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fool

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, 10 stocks we like better than AGNC Investment Corp.
  • AGNC (AGNC -0.53%), the second-largest mortgage real estate investment trust (mREIT), pays a massive forward dividend yield of 18.3%.
  • Unlike equity real estate investment trusts (REITs), which purchase properties and rent them out, mREITs invest in mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and other mortgage-related products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Leo Sun – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:45AM EST.

According to recent reports, 10 stocks we like better than AGNC Investment Corp. ›.

AGNC (AGNC -0.53%), the second-largest mortgage real estate investment trust (mREIT), pays a massive forward dividend yield of 18.3%. That high yield might seem tempting, but investors should understand what an mREIT is -- and why it isn't for everyone.

Unlike equity real estate investment trusts (REITs), which purchase properties and rent them out, mREITs invest in mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and other mortgage-related products. By borrowing money at short-term rates to buy longer-term mortgage-related assets, it generates a profit from the spread between its borrowing costs and asset yields.

AGNC primarily invests in Agency MBS, which are backed by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, or Ginnie Mae. That government support makes it less risky than other mREITs, including Annaly Capital (NLY -0.74%), which allocate more of their portfolios to non-Agency MBS. mREITs, like REITs, must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income as dividends for a lower tax rate.

NASDAQ · As of 9:40 AM ET 11/19/26.

However, mREITs only flourish when interest rates are low. Abrupt rate hikes erode their book value per share and net spread and dollar roll income per share (which funds their dividends).

From 2021 to 2025, AGNC's book value per share dropped from $15.75 to $8.88; its annual dividends stayed unchanged at $1.44 per share, but its net spread and dollar roll income per share fell from $3.11 in 2021 to $1.50 in 2025.

That decline, largely driven by the Fed's 11 rate hikes in 2022 and 2023, caused its stock to plunge 51% over the past five years. With reinvested dividends, it delivered a nearly flat total return. So before you buy AGNC for its massive yield, you should be aware of these long-term risks.

#39176. iFixit Notes Apple’s HomeView Breaks Easily. Here’s Why I’m Not Worried

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (672 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

iFixit Notes Apple’s HomeView Breaks Easily. Here’s Why I’m Not Worried

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for the past few years, Apple was looking almost DIY-friendly.
  • Industry observers note that the good news?
  • DIY repairs are a big deal for Apple products, not just because they’re difficult, but because many people believe they have a right to repair their own phones or computers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for the past few years, Apple was looking almost DIY-friendly. The company had been moving toward smart speakers that you could take apart without damaging and iPads with accessible batteries. But the new HomeView smart display broke apart when iFixit tried to access components in Tuesday’s full analysis.

Industry observers note that the good news? I don’t think it really matters, at least not for this particular Apple device. Here’s why.

DIY repairs are a big deal for Apple products, not just because they’re difficult, but because many people believe they have a right to repair their own phones or computers.

Making repairs more accessible also sustains a secondary market of iPhone and Mac repair services that Apple would rather tightly control — or squash entirely. That’s one reason the EU has required Apple to make iPhone batteries replaceable in 2027.

In a recent development, the HomeView moves sharply in the opposite direction, held together by the toughest adhesive iFixit has ever encountered in an Apple product. The glue is so stubborn that the team accidentally snapped a speaker in half during disassembly, and the logic board was bound too dangerously tight to the aluminum chassis to remove.

Industry observers note that “Obviously, when you buy a product you don’t anticipate the accidents, and there’s no way of knowing when wear and tear will become a problem,” iFixit said in its report. “But you can be sure of one thing: The HomeView will not be an easy or pleasant repair when that time comes.”.

A representative from Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

iFixit also pointed out that if a HomeView device falls out of warranty, the repair typically costs as much as the $299 smart display itself.

I’m just not sure any potential HomeView users need to worry about the device’s repairability the way they would about an iPhone or Mac.

Smart displays don’t have the same DIY repair needs as the phone in your pocket. There’s no battery to replace, which is one of the most common reasons to open up an iPhone or MacBook. And while a shattered iPhone screen can easily be swapped out for a third-party replacement, no aftermarket alternatives exist for the HomeView’s custom 7-inch display. Since you can only get a replacement screen through Apple anyway, making the device easier to open wouldn’t actually help you fix it yourself.

Recent findings suggest that plus, smart displays don’t face the same environmental risks as phones and laptops, which are constantly on the move, encounter dust in pockets, accidentally dropped and exposed to potential heat and rain. The HomeView is designed to remain stationary in your home. The need for DIY repairs is simply far less of a concern.

Industry observers note that I don’t mean to say iFixit’s teardown was unnecessary. We learned valuable information, including how the speakers and their connectors broke in several ways when iFixit tried to remove them. (The speaker assembly is actually one HomeView component I worry people may need to replace.).

It has been revealed that “Embedded speakers are a relatively common source of failure. The under-screen speakers inside the HomeView in particular, more closely resemble laptop speakers than HomePod tweeters,” the iFixit report notes. “As far as laptop and MacBook speakers go, we’ve seen plenty of examples of damage caused by accidents and wear and tear.”.

I’ve been testing smart displays and smart speakers since they first hit the market, and none of the devices I’ve tested have developed a blown or faulty speaker. In the HomePod subreddit, I couldn’t find any reports of speaker failures except from people already Frankensteining their Apple speakers with third-party components.

Industry observers note that I wouldn’t let the fear of repair difficulties get in the way of buying a HomeView. A bigger concern is the HomeView’s compact 7-inch screen, which feels cramped for watching video, especially compared with the larger displays Amazon has rolled out across its Echo Show lineup.

#39173. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we all know AI can get expensive.
  • Also: Microsoft indicates its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft indicates its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

Recent findings suggest that if it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s substantial bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Sources indicate that software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

According to recent reports, then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s latest.

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

According to recent reports, there’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically claims, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving manufacturer labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the organization saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

I find it particularly telling that this is from the firm that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

It has been revealed that microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the firm’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

It has been revealed that this means the organization doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

CRYPTO · As of 9:42 AM ET 11/19/26.

#39170. Industry News: Scout Motors Is Using AI Earpieces to Train Factory Workers

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (998 w)

Industry News: Scout Motors Is Using AI Earpieces to Train Factory Workers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “AI training” usually refers to instilling artificial intelligence with human knowledge.
  • CEO Scott Keogh spoke with CNET during a reporters roundtable at Scout’s still-under-construction factory in Blythewood, South Carolina.
  • Keogh described the approach as starting from the work itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“AI training” usually refers to instilling artificial intelligence with human knowledge. Scout Motors notes it’s been doing the opposite: using AI tools to help hire, onboard and train factory workers, including an AI assistant in an earpiece that guides trainees through tasks as they perform them.

CEO Scott Keogh spoke with CNET during a reporters roundtable at Scout’s still-under-construction factory in Blythewood, South Carolina. Keogh said that rather than “sitting new hires down with an instructional binder and a test,” workers are getting AI-driven, hands-on experience early in a push to make the training more efficient and effective. Meanwhile, the automaker can collect and feed training data back into the system to fine-tune its hiring, training and placement processes.

Keogh described the approach as starting from the work itself. Manufacturing, he said, can be broken down into a handful of fundamental tasks, and the AI system is built to teach each one. He offered parts picking as the simplest example: A worker walks to 12 boxes, pulls 12 parts, confirms they’re in the right sequence and checks them for defects. The AI in the earpiece can guide the worker through that sequence, providing real-time, adaptable instructions.

“We can train that within minutes,” Keogh said. “A worker repeats the cycle about 15 times, getting faster and better each pass, and then moves down the task line to the next skill.”.

To my ears, that doesn’t sound like the sort of task you’d need an AI system to help with and, to some extent, Scout’s executives agreed.

Industry observers note that however, the automaker’s representatives argued that the new method is far more productive than traditional classroom training — with increasing benefits as the trained tasks and concepts become more complex. Keogh also linked the speed at which the company has seen its newest factory hires become productive with how rapidly Scout can ramp up the factory itself.

According to recent reports, scout execs say AI also plays a role in the hiring and onboarding before training begins. Todd Johnson, vice president of manufacturing, mentioned the team feeds new hires’ backgrounds into an AI system, which suggests where each person might fit best: A former forklift driver might be steered toward logistics, someone with no final assembly experience might do better in the body shop and a person with paint shop experience could be placed as a painter.

Again, that sounded a lot like common sense to me. Isn’t that how people were hired before AI? According to Scout Motors’ leadership, the algorithm can potentially identify less obvious connections between skills and tasks that a human might miss, expanding access to jobs for applicants who may not have received traditional manufacturing training, which is notable because Scout’s newly introduced plant is located in an area that doesn’t have a large pool of local dyed-in-the-wool traditional automotive workers.

Recent findings suggest that to fill the over 4,000 roles that factory will need to reach full speed ahead by 2028, the automaker states it’s hiring from a national pool of applicants. However, executives told me that using AI to consider nontraditional factory workers — citing one hire who worked at the DMV — will allow Scout to identify and place more local applicants and bring fresh ideas to the factory floor.

Industry observers note that ryan Decker, vice president of strategy and brand, called Scout’s AI-forward approach to placement and training “a passion project for the tech giant.” Decker told CNET that Scout’s training AI can tailor instruction to each person rather than delivering the same material to a room of 10 people over 10 days. People learn differently, he said, with different language skills and levels of technical depth.

According to recent reports, decker also said the system is bidirectional. The AI can learn from how each group responds to the training and use that information to modify instruction for the next cohort. Decker thinks that each subsequent batch of workers will be “1% better,” and that after 1,000 repetitions, he expects the AI to be “dialed in and know how to provide information to the people in the most productive way possible.”.

Scout indicates it’s also exploring vision-based AI training, in which the trainee is guided via augmented reality glasses, as the next evolution of the technology. The automaker is also looking to eventually expand the tech for do-it-yourself use by owners at home. I imagine a future where owners can use an Apple Vision Pro or similar device — which would be a pricey investment — to guide themselves through installing a roof rack or performing routine maintenance.

In practice, the next step, according to Scout’s execs, is to scale its AI learning tools beyond the training room and into the actual factory and service centers, where the automaker believes the tech can continue to improve on-the-floor productivity and guide its workers as they advance through their careers.

Decker states the AI can ingest and organize decades of institutional knowledge, making it accessible to workers during and beyond the training process. Scout has been feeding the AI equipment manuals and manufacturing documentation spanning multiple decades, disciplines and countries — what Decker called “hundreds of years of accumulated enterprise know-how” — which the AI earpiece can surface in real time, something he mentioned was near impossible to do before in a world of binders and PDFs.

Recent findings suggest that scout’s AI-fueled “passion project” arrives amid broader tensions across industries affected by artificial intelligence. Companies are eager for the efficiencies AI promises, while workers worry the same technology could eventually cost them their jobs. Scout’s executives didn’t address that concern directly in this exchange. Keogh framed the payoff in terms of speed — how swiftly a new hire can be made productive — leaving the wider workforce conversation for another time.

It has been revealed that editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Scout Motors. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the tech giant’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft claims its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the tech giant’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft claims its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

According to recent reports, “As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also revealed Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft noted, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft mentioned the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

Industry observers note that “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

Industry observers note that the company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

According to recent reports, nadella also revealed a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

Microsoft also revealed that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft unveiled a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

In a recent development, agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the firm’s observability platform. Microsoft mentioned Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft demonstrated how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

According to recent reports, “It starts with a fresh way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft remarked. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft stated. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise prepares.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chase is growing its roster of airline transfer partners to include Qantas Frequent Flyer and Cathay Pacific Asia Miles.

It has been revealed that that’ll bump the number of Chase’s transfer partners to 16, with 12 airline and four hotel loyalty programs. The new partners, which are live as of Nov. 18, 2026, will transfer at a 1:1 ratio from Chase Ultimate Rewards®.

You’ll need an eligible Chase card, such as the Chase Sapphire Reserve® and the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card, to transfer points.

Qantas and Cathay Pacific are the flag carriers for Australia and Hong Kong, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that both airlines are part of the Oneworld alliance, which includes U.S. carriers like American Airlines, Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. They also maintain relationships with non-alliance partners.

Sources indicate that your best shot at award seats on Qantas and Cathay Pacific flights is often through their own programs. That’s because airlines typically release the most award availability to their own loyalty program members.

While some partner airline programs might offer cheaper award pricing, it can be harder to find award availability through them. That’s why having points and miles with the airline you want to fly on can be so valuable.

Sources indicate that this is especially helpful for airlines that operate highly sought-after routes or premium cabin products. For example, Cathay Pacific's Aria Suite in business class is a popular choice for flyers. It's available on select flights from Hong Kong to North America, Europe, Australia and parts of Asia, so check the seat map before booking. For example, Cathay Pacific’s Aria Suite in business class is a popular choice for flyers and is only available on select routes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Qantas is expected to start flying the world's longest commercial route in October 2027 between Sydney and London, as part of its Project Sunrise initiative. It’s also slated to launch nonstop flights between Sydney and Newly introduced York the following year.

Those seats aren’t on sale yet, but they’re likely to be highly coveted for award travelers.

These additions aren’t particularly exciting if you already have access to other transferable currencies like Capital One miles, which transfer 1:1 to both Qantas and Cathay Pacific.

However, if you’re all in on Chase points, these upcoming airline partners can unlock more award redemption opportunities.

It has been revealed that the best way to earn a large tranche of Chase points is through a welcome offer, available to fresh applicants on select cards. If you’re looking to add a card that earns Chase points to your wallet, here are some options:.

• 5x points on all Chase Travel℠ purchases (exclusions apply).

• 5x on Lyft rides and Peloton equipment (for a limited time; terms apply).

#39165. At Scout Motors’ Fresh Plant, Validation of Terra and Traveler EVs Has Begun

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (837 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

At Scout Motors’ Fresh Plant, Validation of Terra and Traveler EVs Has Begun

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, at Scout Motors’ South Carolina Production Center, the automaker’s very first electrified trucks and SUVs are being welded, painted and assembled.
  • Recent findings suggest that after a period of slow sales, American interest in electric vehicles and hybrids is on the rise, driven by high fuel costs and the steady growth of EV charging infrastructure in 2026.
  • I donned my hardhat, steel-toe caps and high-vis vest to get an early look inside the plant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at Scout Motors’ South Carolina Production Center, the automaker’s very first electrified trucks and SUVs are being welded, painted and assembled. The revived American automaker has begun the first validation builds of its upcoming Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV at the Blythewood plant, but hold your electric horses — final production and customer deliveries are still a little over a year away.

Recent findings suggest that after a period of slow sales, American interest in electric vehicles and hybrids is on the rise, driven by high fuel costs and the steady growth of EV charging infrastructure in 2026. Scout, with its battery-electric and gasoline range-extended powertrains, could have both of those bases covered when it arrives to compete in America’s most popular vehicle classes (trucks and SUVs) in 2028. It’s worth keeping an eye on Scout as it inches toward production.

I donned my hardhat, steel-toe caps and high-vis vest to get an early look inside the plant.

The Volkswagen Group revived the Scout Motors brand (formerly International Scout) in 2022, and in 2024, the public got its first look at the Terra and Traveler concepts. The two were initially revealed as full-electric models with the option to add Scout’s Harvester onboard gasoline generator to boost the range.

However, demand for the extended-range EV configuration was overwhelming — roughly 87% of the 160,000-plus reservation holders selected the Harvester spec over the all-electric version — and Scout pivoted to delivering the EREV first, then following up with the pure battery-electric model later in production.

Both models are expected to start under $60,000, though Scout has not yet confirmed the exact price difference between the Harvester and pure BEV trims.

In early 2024, the automaker broke ground on the Blythewood Production Center, pledging to invest more than $2 billion in the plant and create more than 4,000 local jobs. A year later, Scout declared plans to add a $300 million supplier park to the complex, supporting around 1,000 on-site jobs at parts suppliers.

According to recent reports, today, construction is mostly complete. (Executives told me it’s about 80% to 95% done, depending on how you measure it.) The walls are up, much of the equipment is in place, and the first movement toward full production of the brand’s extended-range EV and, eventually, battery electric trucks and SUVs has begun.

Scout’s manufacturing and production teams have begun building the first validation builds — early-stage preproduction vehicles that allow factory planners to dial in vehicle quality, confirm the accuracy of the engineering and hone the efficiency of the manufacturing and assembly lines.

These aren’t complete vehicles by any stretch, being pulled from the line at various points to check and double-check that the new factory equipment functions properly and that the right parts arrive when and where they’re needed. Executives warned me that, at this point, there would still be inconsistencies as they dial in panel gaps, welds and the application of various coatings, but that Scout expects the process to be dialed in by the time full production starts in late 2027.

I was able to get up close to these validation vehicles, checking out a body-in-white bare chassis in the body shop, seeing various stages of coatings applied to bare metal, and watching workers complete calibration and alignment of lights and sensors in the final assembly area.

Sources indicate that along the way, Scout told me that more than 160 individual parts must come together to form the vehicle’s chassis, a process supported by more than 750 robots and 5,000 weld points. Once up to speed, the factory body shop is designed to produce around 40 vehicles per hour, with pickups and SUVs sharing the same line.

In a recent development, however, while I saw the robotic welding arms and paint sprayers performing their motions to apply color, no vehicles were actually moving through the assembly line. This early in the process, the automaker doesn’t need a continuous flow of validation vehicles, and many of the factory areas — such as the supplier park that will provide the batteries, electric motors and modified VW Group four-cylinder engines for Harvester models — are still under construction.

Additionally, the validation process gives workers hands-on experience, rather than having them learn from mistakes on cars that will reach customers or being confined to a classroom.

According to recent reports, as more parts of the factory complete construction and come online, the validation process will encompass more of the vehicle’s construction until the automaker is ready to start building full customer vehicles. Todd Johnson, Scout’s vice president of manufacturing, tells me that validation will continue into 2027 through multiple preproduction phases starting with the Traveler SUV.

The automaker expects the first customer deliveries of the Traveler Harvester to begin in early 2028, followed by the Terra Harvester and, eventually, fully electric versions of both.

Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Scout Motors. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Should You Buy Micron Technology Stock While It's Under $1,000? The Answer Might Surprise You.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Micron Technology (MU +5.91%) is one of the world's top suppliers of high bandwidth memory (HBM) for data centers, which is a critical part of the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware stack.
  • It has been revealed that AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic continue to raise prices for the use of their models to offset soaring infrastructure costs, forcing many end owners to cap their usage.
  • In a recent development, micron stock is down by 40% from its June peak, and closed at $719.02 on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anthony Di Pizio – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:03AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

Micron Technology (MU +5.91%) is one of the world's top suppliers of high bandwidth memory (HBM) for data centers, which is a critical part of the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware stack. The company has experienced more demand than it can possibly supply over the last few years, but investors are increasingly worried about a slowdown in the AI boom.

It has been revealed that AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic continue to raise prices for the use of their models to offset soaring infrastructure costs, forcing many end owners to cap their usage. Moreover, Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive officer of Nvidia last week after a series of extramarital affairs came to light, one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy, casting a cloud of uncertainty over the entire AI industry.

In a recent development, micron stock is down by 40% from its June peak, and closed at $719.02 on Nov. 16. Is this a golden opportunity for investors to buy it under $1,000, or is there more downside ahead? Read on for the surprising answer.

HBM keeps data flowing seamlessly to graphics processing units (GPUs), which are the main chips used in AI workloads. Bottlenecks would ensue without sufficient memory, because GPUs would be forced to pause their workloads while they wait to receive more data. This would create a sluggish experience for customers of AI chatbots, agents, and other applications.

Personal computers, smartphones, and even cars also require an increasing amount of memory capacity to run certain AI workloads locally on-device, and Micron is also one of the top suppliers in each of those categories.

In a recent development, micron generated $133.2 billion in total revenue during its 2026 fiscal year (ended Sept. 3), an eye-popping 256% increase from the previous year. AI-related memory demand was responsible for the strong result, positively impacting all four of the company's business segments.

Data source: Micron Technology.

The cloud memory segment is where Micron accounts for memory sales to hyperscale customers (like Amazon and Microsoft), as well as HBM sales for all data center customers. The core data center segment, on the other hand, includes sales of storage and non-HBM memory solutions to data center customers.

According to recent reports, the cloud memory business is most at risk if there is a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending. None of the hyperscalers have revealed looks to reduce their investments in data centers yet, which is a positive sign. But price hikes from AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic could start feeding through to demand.

In a recent development, over the last few months, Walmart, Amazon, and Uber Technologies are just some of the companies that have placed restrictions on internal AI usage to prevent budget blowouts, amid rising costs. Questions are also mounting about AI adoption among consumers, with Uber recently saying almost nobody is using agents on its platform.

It has been revealed that the recent midterm elections might also be a headwind for AI infrastructure spending. The newly introduced Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas looks to pause future data center approvals until new legislation is in place to protect local communities from issues like rising electricity costs and water scarcity. Texas is one of America's top destinations for data center construction, so this could be problematic for semiconductor companies like Micron.

In a recent development, there is right now more demand for HBM than Micron and its peers can supply, which is giving them the ability to dictate prices. As a result, Micron's earnings rocketed higher by 879% year over year to $74.33 during fiscal 2026, placing its stock at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 9.7. That is one-third of the P/E of the Nasdaq-100 index, which is 29.5, so the stock appears incredibly undervalued.

NASDAQ · As of 9:37 AM ET 11/19/26.

Industry observers note that moreover, Wall Street thinks Micron could grow its earnings to $176.50 per share in fiscal 2027, placing its stock at a forward P/E ratio of just 4.1. It seems almost ludicrous that a manufacturer growing as fast as Micron would be trading at such a steep discount to the broader market. However, the semiconductor industry has always been highly cyclical, so investors know AI-related demand won't continue at this pace forever.

It has been revealed that micron and its peers are racing to build more manufacturing capacity, which will ease supply constraints and put downward pressure on memory prices. Combine that with the potential demand headwinds I highlighted earlier, and it becomes clear that Micron probably won't be able to sustain its current level of earnings for the long term. That means its stock might be more expensive than it currently appears at face value.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, I personally don't proposal to buy Micron stock at the current price. The level of uncertainty is simply too high for my liking.

Microsoft’s upcoming Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, during the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company.
  • Also: Microsoft claims its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.
  • Sources indicate that MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, during the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft claims its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.

Sources indicate that MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, stated during the keynote.

Sources indicate that the approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft remarked it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

According to recent reports, the dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Sources indicate that western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026.

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman mentioned of the new coding model the tech giant declared at Ignite.

The organization also released its fresh image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.
